#5390. Garlinghouse: 2026 Is Phenomenal Year for Ripple

Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse has called 2026 a "phenomenal" year for the company as it witnesses a significant increase in transaction volumes and business activities.

The Ripple boss has emphasized that the company has witnessed a huge surge in its transaction volumes in the last year, showing the rising demand for its blockchain-based financial infrastructure.

Garlinghouse further reiterated his big plans for XRP as he foresees the crypto eventually becoming an institutional gold standard for crypto payment rails.

Nevertheless, Garlinghouse admitted that XRP may not necessarily be ideal for all financial transactions.

Garlinghouse is clear that Ripple will continue to focus on XRP for cases where the crypto is clearly advantageous.

He stated that it makes good business sense for the company.

Garlinghouse argues that XRP doesn't necessarily need to be the solution for all the transactions that happen on Ripple's infrastructure to be commercially viable.

"We think that XRP is very efficient in some use cases. Probably not in other use cases. But that's ok," he said.

The Ripple CEO is more than okay with XRP being utilized for a small portion of customer transactions.

"That's great. That still means that I am getting some of the pie," he added.

"Sometimes I think people get a little fixated on how big the piece is and how big the pie is," he added.

With his remarks, Garlinghouse seems to suggest that Ripple's approach with XRP is a very pragmatic one. The company is focused on growing its business and finding cases where XRP can be truly beneficial.

Meanwhile, David Schwartz, Ripple's CTO emeritus and one of the co-creators of the XRP Ledger, has made a bold prediction for the future of blockchain technology.

Schwartz was asked about where he sees XRP and Ripple in 5 years. Schwartz sees mass retail adoption ahead.

Schwartz also foresees blockchain technology being just as prevalent and fundamental to life as the internet.

Garlinghouse's positive outlook comes as Ripple is celebrating the 10th edition of its biggest event — the Swell conference in New York City from Oct. 27–29.

A lot of announcements have already come out of the event, showcasing Ripple's growing ambitions in the institutional finance sphere.

The big one includes U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's appearance. He sat down with Garlinghouse to talk about the future of digital assets and the American financial system.

Ripple also announced a big partnership with Robinhood to bring more RLUSD stablecoin and infrastructure use cases. The partnership focuses on institutional settlement, prime brokerage, and treasury use cases.

The company also deepened its relationship with the banking giant BNY. The expanded collaboration includes digital asset custody and tokenized trade finance using XRP, RLUSD, and the XRP Ledger.

Also, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency finally approved Ripple National Trust Bank's last regulatory hurdle.

On top of that, Coinbase has agreed to bring more RLUSD availability to the exchange's retail and institutional platforms.

All the announcements come with impressive growth numbers that Ripple has shared.

Per the company, Ripple is on its way to ending 2026 with roughly $900M in annualized product revenue. Also, Ripple has reported a 3x increase in the number of customers and partners that are using multiple products from Ripple's expanding product line.

The company's financial infrastructure is used by over 1,700 institutions, corporations, and enterprises.

With all the developments, it's no surprise that Garlinghouse is particularly bullish on Ripple's future as the company tries to carve out its spot in a rapidly changing financial services landscape.

#5387. Coinbase CEO Predicts End of Subscription Era

Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong is predicting that stablecoins and AI will reshape the way consumers pay for content on the internet, upending the subscription model that powers much of the web.

Armstrong posited this idea in an X post, where he claimed that stablecoins combined with the new x402 payment protocol will improve usability for businesses and consumers when it comes to micropayments for usage.

"Stablecoins and x402 enable businesses to accept micropayments for usage and decrease friction at checkout," the Coinbase CEO said.

Armstrong was particularly bullish on how x402 could disrupt online news subscriptions.

He argued that people shouldn't have to buy a monthly subscription just to read one article.

Instead, an AI agent could be tasked with retrieving the article on a consumer's behalf and would pay the publisher for that specific piece of content on autopilot.

The x402 technology powering Armstrong's vision is an open payment protocol that was first introduced by Coinbase in May 2025.

x402 is a reference to the HTTP 402 status code, meaning "Payment Required."

Although HTTP 402 has been around since the early days of the internet, it was never widely used for payments.

Coinbase's x402 protocol is designed to turn this largely dormant element of HTTP into an automated payment process that can facilitate transactions between websites, applications, and AI agents.

To illustrate, say you wanted an AI assistant to pull a certain article from a newspaper. Let's say it's priced at $0.25.

At this point, the AI agent can send a payment authorization for $0.25 in stablecoins, assuming the user has given the agent permission to make these payments.

Armstrong's views come as Coinbase and other big tech firms are pushing ahead with the infrastructure needed to facilitate AI payments.

In June, Coinbase teamed up with Amazon Web Services to enable publishers who use AWS CloudFront and Web Application Firewall to monetize the requests of AI agents through x402.

Separately, Cloudflare introduced its Monetization Gateway in closed beta in September. This allows participating businesses to request payments from AI agents for access to websites, datasets, and application programming interfaces through the x402 protocol.

#5386. JPMorgan and Coca-Cola Block Tokenized Stocks on OKXICE as Objectors Hit 33. Coinbase and Robinhood Stay Out of the List

All reviews, research, news and assessments of any kind on The Tokenist are compiled using a strict editorial review process by our editorial team. JPMorgan Chase, AMD, Coca-Cola and four other companies have barred tokenized versions of their shares from OKXICE, the planned venue for tokenized stocks from OKX and NYSE owner Intercontinental Exchange, in a notice dated Tuesday, October 27. That brings the objectors to 33 of the 62 companies the venue first named, worth roughly $17 trillion.

One group is missing from the list. Coinbase, Robinhood, Circle, and Strategy, the crypto stocks among the 62, have not objected, and their own businesses depend in part on putting assets on blockchains.

So why is Wall Street saying no while crypto companies stay in?

More than half of the original list, and the pace has picked up. OKXICE’s first notice, dated October 4, named 63 stocks from 62 companies. Its October 19 notice listed 16 objectors. By October 27 there were 33, including Microsoft, Alphabet, Broadcom, Goldman Sachs, Wells Fargo, Oracle, Intel and IBM.

Issuer objections in each OKXICE public notice. Source: OKXICE

The latest seven were JPMorgan, AMD, Applied Materials, Coca-Cola, Adobe, Dell and SanDisk. JPMorgan stands out: it runs its own blockchain unit, Kinexys, and issues deposit tokens for institutional clients, but it still doesn’t want an outside firm tokenizing its shares.

$17 TRILLION worth of stocks now rejects TOKENIZATION.7 more companies have objected to digital token versions of their shares on OKXICE:1. JPMorgan $JPM: ~$890B2. AMD $AMD: ~$870B3. Coca-Cola $KO: ~$400B4. Dell $DELL: ~$320B5. Applied Materials $AMAT: ~$310B6. Sandisk… https://t.co/jmvXXrkJt5

The rule behind the objections is simple. Under the SEC’s September 17 exemption, a venue that wants to list a stock tokenized by an unaffiliated third party must notify the issuer, which then has 30 days to object. An objection keeps that token off the venue. It doesn’t stop tokenized versions trading elsewhere.

On OKXICE, each token would be backed one-for-one by a real share held by a registered broker-dealer, carry the same dividends and voting rights, and trade around the clock against stablecoins on OKX’s X Layer network. OKXICE co-chair Andrew Cuomo called the objections a “natural response” from companies taking a wait-and-see approach.

All four of the best-known. Coinbase, Robinhood, Circle and Strategy were named in OKXICE’s first notice, and none appears among the 33 objectors. Custody firm BitGo and tokenization company Securitize were also on the list, Benzinga reported, and haven’t objected either.

Their shares have had a rough month regardless:

October 2 was the last trading day before the first notice. Prices: Yahoo Finance, premarket at 13:00 UTC.

Two of the objectors have crypto roots. CoreWeave began as an Ethereum miner and Applied Digital as a host for Bitcoin miners. Both now sell computing power to AI companies, and both were among the first nine to object.

None of them has said, and staying off the list isn’t the same as signing up. OKXICE doesn’t say when each issuer was notified, so some 30-day windows may still be open. But objecting would sit awkwardly with what these companies sell.

The objectors haven’t explained themselves either. Their industry has, in part. SIFMA, the main Wall Street trade group, asked the SEC on October 19 to consider requiring companies’ consent before their shares are tokenized, a longer objection period, and a single opt-out that would apply to every venue. Questions about who counts as a shareholder, how votes and corporate actions pass through, and how much trading can move on-chain are still open.

Discover: SEC Filing Outlines 24/7 Plan for 63 OKX Tokenized Stocks

Earnings, more than tokenization. Robinhood reported on Tuesday evening: revenue rose 12% to a record $1.42 billion and equity trading volume jumped 53% to $992 billion, but crypto revenue fell 55% to $120 million. Its shares were down 6% before Wednesday’s open, at $88.90.

Coinbase and Strategy report after the close on Thursday, October 29. With Bitcoin near $81,000, down about 36% from its October 2025 peak, both will be judged on how much the slower crypto market has cost them.

OKXICE, for its part, hasn’t set a launch date, and each new notice so far has added objectors. Of the 29 companies that haven’t objected, four are crypto stocks.

Discover: Bitcoin and Gold Are 2026’s Worst Asset Classes So Far, and Crypto Stocks Have Fared Worse: Can Coinbase and Strategy Earnings Change the Story This Week?

For tokenized stocks, the next OKXICE notice will show whether the objections keep coming. For crypto stocks, Thursday’s earnings will matter more.

#5385. Stellar Opens Two-Way Bridge to Ethereum as Institutional RWA Gains Momentum on Network

Stellar has unveiled an upgraded two-way Ethereum bridge to improve application interoperability across its network and other blockchain ecosystems.

To advance interoperability, Stellar has opened a two-way bridge to Ethereum, integrating its protocol with Ethereum’s mainnet. According to market development released today, Stellar revealed the launch of VIA Labs’ cross-chain messaging system on its mainnet.

Stellar’s move to open the VIA Labs’ multichain bridge on its protocol gives its Soroban smart contract platform direct, two-way communication with Ethereum. The connection now lets smart contracts on both Stellar and Ethereum exchange messages and applications through VIA Labs’ multichain messaging system.

The cross-chain bridge integration matters in several ways. As the announcement states, it lets Stellar developers efficiently move supported applications and assets between networks. It also enables developers to orchestrate contract activities across chains, including building applications around stablecoins and tokenized real-world assets.

Meanwhile, the multichain bridge addresses fragmentation on Stellar by letting users move assets and interact efficiently with different blockchain environments, including the Ethereum ecosystem.

The two-way Ethereum bridge integrates at a time when the RWA narrative continues to gain momentum on Stellar. The network is rapidly emerging as a major force in the race to tokenize RWAs, with billions of dollars flocking into the blockchain.

This is evident in Securitize, the largest tokenization platform, which has integrated the Stellar network to issue and manage its tokenized financial assets. Other dominant global asset managers that recently moved tokenized funds to Stellar include Pontoro, ArchaxEX, among others, underscoring the network’s growing popularity.

By unveiling the groundbreaking two-way Ethereum bridge, Stellar addresses the complex engineering challenge in RWA tokenization. To accurately represent physical commodities, bonds, real estate, and more on the blockchain, Stellar needs not only strong, interoperable smart contracts but also a flawless, tamper-proof data bridge. This is where the two-way Ethereum bridge comes in.

A 5x long is a risky position. With four million USDC deposited and only about $1.77 million used as the position size, the trader has plenty of extra margin. That puts the liquidation price far below the current market price, so a small drop will not wipe out the trade. This suggests the trader plans to hold through volatility rather than gamble on a quick bounce.

Large new wallets like this one often draw attention because they can signal confidence from a big player. Still, one trade does not decide where the price goes. Whales can be wrong, and they can close positions quickly.

Traders should watch the $577 area first. If XMR holds there and climbs back above $600, the uptrend remains intact and another test of $620 to $660 becomes likely. If the price breaks below $577, a drop toward $552 is the next logical target. For now, Monero remains in a strong uptrend that is taking a short break. The whale long adds to the bullish story, but the price must reclaim $600 to confirm that buyers are back in control.

Decentralized platform Hyperliquid has permanently removed 49.87 million native HYPE tokens from circulation, which amounts to almost 5% of its maximum supply of 1 billion units. On-chain monitoring confirms that the combined fiat value of the destroyed assets has reached $3.89 billion at the current market rate.

The supply reduction happens automatically: the protocol converts fee revenue into continuous token buybacks from the open market as the platform's historical revenue has surpassed the $1.38 billion mark.

The mechanism relies on the Assistance Fund, a system smart contract without private keys, whose balance was officially recognized as burned in December 2025 by a decision of 85% of the network's validators. Between 97% and 99% of the exchange's trading fees are directed here.

Over the past 24 hours, this engine destroyed 19,700 HYPE (about $1.59 million) against daily protocol fees of $1.69 million. Of the platform's $1.38 billion in total revenue, $63.52 million was generated over the past 30 days.

In addition to standard trading fees, Hyperliquid's architecture uses additional automated deflation channels:

Since the buyback is strictly denominated in US dollars, the exact rate of token destruction fluctuates depending on the market. At current asset prices of around $78–$80, the net volume of tokens withdrawn per dollar of fees decreases.

The ecosystem's long-term deflationary status now directly depends on whether fee generation can consistently outpace the scheduled vesting for the team and early contributors, which adds about 9.9 million HYPE tokens to circulation every month.

At the current pace of 19,700 tokens per day, buybacks would absorb roughly 591,000 HYPE per month, offsetting only about 6% of these unlocks, which means net circulating supply is still expanding despite the burn.

#5382. CFTC Sets December 14 Deadline to Rewrite "Actual Delivery": Where Exchanges Are Exposed

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The clock is officially ticking on the Commodity Futures Trading Commission’s (CFTC) attempt to overhaul its regulatory grip on retail digital asset trading.

While corporate press releases focused on preliminary announcements, the formal publication of Federal Register Document 2026-20888 under RIN 3038-AF80 establishes a strict deadline: public comments close on December 14, 2026.

That date anchors an urgent operational check for digital asset exchanges, custodians, and margin trading desks. While crypto media outlets like The Defiant and TFTC covered the high-level regulatory announcement, this breakdown maps the ANPRM’s exact per-question mechanics directly against the concrete exchange structures they expose. The Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM) represents the Commission’s first attempt to replace its piecemeal enforcement stances with a binding, notice-and-comment framework for "actual delivery" under Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act (CEA).

Responding by December 14 is not merely an exercise in policy debate; it requires market participants to confront the exact legal and technical mechanics where their existing architectures remain exposed.

Under Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the CEA, any leveraged, margined, or financed retail commodity transaction falls under full CFTC futures regulation unless "actual delivery" occurs within 28 days. Centralized exchanges historically operate in a regulatory gray area by executing off-chain, book-entry updates in internal databases and claiming those entries fulfilled delivery requirements.

The proposed Regulation CTX directly targets that operational model. Through the questions inside the ANPRM 2026-20888, the Commission reveals four critical vulnerabilities that exchanges must address before the comment window shuts:

In its analysis of the proposal, law firm Fenwick & West highlights that the ANPRM leaves open a crucial question regarding how the 28-day actual delivery exception applies to fully-paid transactions maintained entirely on an exchange’s internal ledger.

If an exchange's user agreement or onboarding terms contain broad margin or financing language, the CFTC signals that every transaction on the platform, even fully-paid spot trades could be swept into the CTX umbrella. Without explicit actual delivery, an exchange keeping user assets on internal book-entry databases risks having its entire spot book reclassified as an illegal, unregistered derivatives venue.

The ANPRM questions whether off-chain ledger entries can ever satisfy actual delivery without an explicit on-chain transaction. If the CFTC mandates on-chain settlement, exchanges relying on centralized databases to match order books at high speeds will face severe throughput bottlenecks and surging gas costs.

The notice probes what constitutes true "possession and control" by the buyer. The CFTC specifically asks whether a customer maintains full control if an exchange retains administrative keys, emergency pause functions, or liquidation authority. If retaining risk-management hooks breaks the delivery exception, platforms cannot claim actual delivery while maintaining centralized control over user balances.

Recognizing that instant on-chain delivery for high-frequency retail leverage is technically impractical, the Commission seeks feedback on Alternative CTX framework models. The notice asks whether leveraging registered Futures Commission Merchant (FCM) structures, strict account segregation, and proof-of-reserves audits can provide a viable compliance pathway for platforms choosing not to settle every trade on-chain.

Because this ANPRM RIN 3038-AF80 precedes a formal Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM), the CFTC is using the December 14, 2026 window to gather empirical data on how exchanges manage custody, leverage, and settlement. Platforms can review the docket materials directly via the CFTC Innovation page.

Exchanges relying on internal ledgers to offer retail products must submit technical feedback demonstrating how their custody models preserve user protection. Once the CFTC translates these questions into binding NPRM language, the legal definition of "actual delivery" will solidify, leaving non-compliant exchanges directly vulnerable to federal enforcement actions.

About 135,700 Bitcoin options worth $10.9 billion expire on Deribit at 08:00 UTC on Friday, October 30, a third of the exchange’s open contracts, two days after the Federal Reserve held rates in a 10–2 vote that left a December hike open.The price is sitting almost on top of the expiry’s pain point. BTC trades at $79,976, down 1.8% in 24 hours, after giving back its whole post-Fed bounce overnight. Max pain for Friday’s Bitcoin options expiry, the price at which buyers of those contracts would lose the most, is $78,000, and the October low that has held for a week is $79,221.

So what exactly is expiring, how did Bitcoin take the Fed, and can it hold $79,000 through Friday?

🚨 BREAKING: Bitcoin PLUNGES below $80,000 as tech stocks tumble and crypto liquidations hit $335 MILLION in 24 hours. pic.twitter.com/AZRs51zPv2

Mostly bullish bets that are now far out of reach. Deribit’s public order book data at 09:01 UTC on Thursday shows 135,676 BTC in contracts dated October 30, out of 397,442 BTC across all Deribit expiries:

Deribit BTC open interest expiring October 30, by strike. Source: Deribit

The Deribit Volatility Index (DVOL), which tracks the 30-day volatility priced into Bitcoin options, fell to 36 from 38 over the past two days. Options traders are paying less for protection even with an expiry this size a day away. Ether adds a smaller expiry of about 338,000 ETH, roughly $780 million.

Discover: BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Managed Protection ETF Would Trade Bitcoin’s Upside for a 10% Floor: Who Is It Built For?

A two-hour rally, then a slow leak. The Fed’s statement on Wednesday kept the federal funds rate at 3.75% to 4%, with Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack voting for a quarter-point hike instead. Chair Kevin Warsh declined to signal the next move: “I don’t believe in forward guidance, absent exigent circumstances, absent a crisis.”

ETF buyers stayed in. U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs took in $137.3 million on Wednesday, their third straight day of inflows, nearly all of it into BlackRock’s IBIT, SoSoValue figures show.

A soft day after the Fed is normal for Bitcoin. On Binance data, BTC was higher 24 hours after only 33 of the Fed’s 71 decisions since January 2018, and after holds the bigger moves tended to come weeks later.

It has so far, but with less room each time. On the 4-hour chart, BTC sits at $80,130, below both its 50-period EMA at $80,978 and its 200-period EMA at $81,635. The faster line crossed under the slower one around October 23, and Wednesday’s post-Fed rally stalled right at the 200 EMA.

The floor is the October 24 low at $79,221. Bitcoin has dipped into the $79,200–$79,850 area on five of the last six days and bounced each time, most recently at 02:00 UTC on Thursday.

Max pain is only a reference point. It marks where option buyers would collect the least on Friday, and the price is under no obligation to go there.

After the Bitcoin options expiry, the next tests come from data, not derivatives: the October jobs report on November 6 and consumer prices on November 10, both on the road to the Fed’s December 9 decision.

Ripple's Swell event kicked off with a bang on October 28, 2026, bringing together decision-makers from traditional finance, crypto, academia and the XRP ecosystem.

In one session highlighted by the official Swell X account, Johann Kerbrat, Senior VP and GM of Crypto at Robinhood, joined Ripple President Monica Long to discuss the evolution of crypto markets, expanding access to digital assets and the future of global financial services.

Tokenization took the main stage at The Shed 🌊 Robinhood's @JohannKerbrat sat down with Ripple President @MonicaLongSF to talk tokenization, crypto markets and what's next for @RobinhoodApp. https://t.co/I7X2E2MMxl

As Robinhood pushes into always-on markets through blockchain technology, the two crypto executives discussed the "unstoppable freight train" of tokenization and what was needed to build the future of global financial services on-chain.

Tokenization involves representing real-world or traditional financial assets as digital tokens on a blockchain, and it is attracting growing attention because it could enable assets to be issued, transferred, and managed through blockchain-based infrastructure.

Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse shares this same viewpoint, saying that as traditional and digital finance converge, market infrastructure is migrating to modern rails. Settlement is moving to real-time, 24/7 and tokenized assets can be traded, financed and used as collateral.

Ripple reported a banner year, with Long commenting on this milestone in an X post: "Our best year ever—approaching $900 million in annualized product revenue run rate exiting 2026, with customers and partners like Standard Chartered, DBS, HSBC, Robinhood, BNY and more using our blockchain infrastructure solutions built with XRPL for a variety of use cases to move, hold, tokenize and deploy assets."

The conversation between the two crypto executives follows a major announcement ahead of the Swell event, which revealed a strategic partnership between Ripple and Robinhood to power the next generation of finance.

Robinhood will integrate Ripple Treasury to modernize and automate its global treasury operations, including cash and liquidity management, cash flow forecasting, payments, risk management, and intercompany netting. The financial services provider will leverage RLUSD on the XRPL for institutional settlement, extending the stablecoin's utility across Bitstamp by Robinhood's growing institutional business.

RLUSD has been listed on Robinhood Chain and Bitstamp by Robinhood and is expected to be available later this year in the Robinhood app.

XRP Ledger activity has jumped to its highest level this year, while the price of XRP slips lower. Active accounts, which count the unique senders on the network, reached 32,604 on October 27. That is the highest reading since the start of 2026 and well above the 30-day average of 19.4K.

For most of the past year, daily active accounts stayed between 13K and 20K. A few short spikes pushed above 30K, but they faded quickly. The latest jump is larger and cleaner than those moves. It also follows a deep drop in late August and early September, when activity fell to nearly 4K accounts.

The numbers have cooled since the peak. The latest reading is 30.5K, down 6.3% in 24 hours, and the chart shows a sharp pullback toward 18K. Even so, the network is far busier than it was a few weeks ago. The all-time high of 106K is still far away, so the ledger has a long way to go before it reaches record levels.

The price chart does not match the surge in usage. XRP trades near $1.29 and has been falling since early October, when it was close to $1.50. The coin is now below the 50-day and 100-day averages, which sit around $1.33 and $1.36. The 200-day average near $1.37 is also above the price. All of these now act as resistance.

Support is near $1.25, where buyers stepped in twice in recent weeks. If that level breaks, the next area to watch is $1.20, followed by the August breakout area near $1.10 to $1.15. Volume has stayed low throughout the decline, and the RSI sits just below 50. This indicates the market is neutral and lacks strong momentum in either direction.

A rise in active accounts can mean more people are using the network for payments, trading, or moving funds. That is a healthy signal for the long term. But network activity does not always push the price up in the short term. Spikes can also come from bots, airdrops, or one-time events, and they often fade quickly, as past peaks this year have shown.

For XRP to turn bullish, the price needs to climb back above $1.33 and then $1.37. Until that happens, the trend remains weak, and the busy ledger stays a positive sign that the market has not yet rewarded.

#5374. The Asterisk on Robinhood Chain’s $51M Win Over Ethereum

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Take 12 days out of Robinhood Chain's first quarter, and the "3-month-old L2 beat Ethereum" headline turns around.

For the other 80 days, Robinhood Chain earned about $166,000 a day in network fees. Ethereum averaged about $446,000.

ARK Invest's numbers are accurate. Robinhood Chain did generate about $51 million in Q3 against Ethereum's roughly $41 million. But the coverage repeated the comparison without checking how the $51 million was made or who ends up with it. Going back to the underlying data, and the comparison holds up much less well than the headline suggests.

ARK's DeFi Quarterly for Q3 2026 charts "Network Real Economic Value by Blockchain". In it, Robinhood Chain logged about $51 million in its first quarter, while Ethereum logged about $41 million, down roughly 35% from the previous quarter.

The comparison spread quickly. A chain that launched on July 1 beating the network that secures most of DeFi made an easy headline. ARK's wider data has more context: total network value across the chains it tracks rose about 24% to roughly $349 million, the first quarterly increase in five quarters, though still about 47% below a year earlier. Robinhood Chain processed about $65 billion in DEX volume, fourth in ARK's dataset, and hosted about $13.7 billion in tokenized equities.

ARK's DeFi Quarterly glossary defines Real Economic Value (REV) as "the total value a network generates consisting of both in-protocol transaction fees and out-of-protocol tips," using data from Blockworks Research.

In other words, both figures measure the same thing: gross fees users paid to use the chain. Robinhood Chain's $51 million matches the $51.0 million in user network fees reported in growthepie's Q3 review of the chain. It's not app revenue. growthepie puts the revenue of apps on Robinhood Chain separately, at $591.4 million.

So ARK didn't mix up its metrics. The trouble is that the same metric means very different things on these two chains. The Q3 number doesn't show that.

growthepie's report has the detail the headline leaves out. A 12-day surge, from August 30 to September 10, pushed median transaction costs to 31 times their pre-surge average. That surge produced 74% of the quarter's fees. growthepie names Relay as the largest tracked fee payer.

Outside the surge, Robinhood Chain earned about 37% of Ethereum's daily rate. At that pace, a full quarter would come to about $15 million, well under Ethereum's $41 million. The "out-earned Ethereum" result depends almost entirely on 12 days when fees jumped to 31 times normal.

That doesn't make the surge fake. Users paid those fees. But the surge came from congestion and higher prices, not steady growth. Across the quarter's 793.7 million transactions, users paid about 6.4 cents per transaction on average. Median costs that briefly rose to 31 times normal aren't a pricing model an exchange-backed chain will want to repeat.

Even with the same metric, the two figures go to very different places.

On Ethereum, most of the $41 million is the base fee, which is burned. That reduces ETH supply and benefits every holder. The rest goes as priority fees and tips to thousands of independent validators. Ethereum's REV is close to a public measure of what the network's users pay.

On Robinhood Chain, an Arbitrum Orbit rollup, fees go to the chain's sequencer, which Robinhood operates. In practice, the $51 million is a company's gross receipts. Some of it goes back to Ethereum to pay for posting data and settling transactions there, and the rest is Robinhood's margin. As coverage of the report noted, how much reaches Robinhood's income statement is still unclear. The company's earnings report on October 27 may answer that.

So on one side, you have fees paid to a decentralized base layer, mostly destroyed. On the other, you have gross receipts for one company, before costs. Both count as "network value," but they aren't the same kind of income.

Three more things make the head-to-head weaker:

The accurate version of the headline is less dramatic: in its first quarter, Robinhood Chain charged its users more in total than Ethereum's base layer did. About three-quarters of that came from a 12-day congestion spike, and the money went to Robinhood's sequencer, not to a decentralized validator set.

That's still a strong debut. Robinhood Chain's stablecoin growth, $13.7 billion in tokenized equities and nearly 800 million transactions are all real. But "beat Ethereum" tells you more about one busy fortnight in early September than about which chain has the stronger business. Q4 will be the real test: without a surge, can Robinhood Chain's fees come close to Ethereum's on an ordinary day?

Dogecoin traders faced fresh pressure amid the ongoing market drop, with 17,833,333 DOGE in long positions liquidated as selling returned to the market. $342 million was liquidated across the crypto market in the last 24 hours, with Dogecoin having its share.

According to CoinGlass data, Dogecoin saw a total of $2.45 million in liquidations over the last 24 hours, with longs accounting for $1.391 million (about 17,833,333 DOGE) of this total, while shorts saw $1.05 million in liquidations.

Long liquidations occur when traders betting on higher prices are forced to close their positions, typically after losses push their margin balances below required levels. When large numbers of leveraged positions are liquidated in a short period, the resulting selling can intensify downward price pressure.

Along these lines, Dogecoin was down nearly 3% in the last 24 hours to $0.078 as the market fell while investors digested the Federal Reserve's decision to hold interest rates steady at its October meeting.

Dogecoin rose for three consecutive days earlier in the week to hit $0.08, but profit-taking in the markets caused its price to retreat.

The Personal Consumption Expenditures Index—the Fed's preferred inflation gauge—was released Thursday, with few cryptocurrencies recouping losses in the wake of the report.

The personal consumption expenditures price index increased a seasonally adjusted 0.5% for the month, putting the annual inflation rate at 3.6% as the pace of price increases stepped up in September, keeping inflation well above the Federal Reserve's target.

While the Fed held interest rates on Wednesday, as expected, two officials dissented in favor of a quarter-point increase and Chair Kevin Warsh declined to signal what might come in December. However, expectations for a 25 basis point hike at the central bank's next meeting on Dec. 9 remain.

If Dogecoin rebounds, the next key resistance levels for Dogecoin are $0.083 and $0.087, while support is envisaged first at $0.074 and $0.069 in the event of a price drop.

The market downturn followed Binance’s disclosure on Thursday of a security incident involving approximately $6.3 billion in crypto assets, according to the report. Notably, the incident even dwarfs the $1.5 billion Bybit breach in 2025, which was attributed to North Korean hackers, making it the biggest crypto hack on record.

Binance co-founder and former CEO Changpeng Zhao, fondly known as CZ, weighed in on the incident, saying on X that it appeared to be a hack. Although he no longer leads the exchange, Zhao remains a major shareholder and an influential figure in the crypto industry.

According to Binance’s preliminary findings, the attacker may have gained access through a DevOps engineer’s compromised laptop, using it to enter a service container and initiate unauthorized withdrawals. The exchange stressed that its investigation had found no evidence of wallet private keys being exposed, suggesting the suspected breach may have exploited internal system access rather than directly compromising the cryptographic keys securing user funds.

The incident has also prompted swift action from major stablecoin issuers. Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino said the company had frozen more than 1.567 billion USDT allegedly linked to the suspected Binance breach, stressing that safeguarding the crypto industry and its partners remained a priority.

Circle CEO Jeremy Allaire separately announced that more than 800 million USDC associated with the incident had been frozen in coordination with law enforcement. Circle said it would continue assisting investigators as they worked to establish what happened.

Meanwhile, Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong revealed the exchange was taking steps to help contain the fallout, including blocking transfers to compromised wallets. In a post on X, Armstrong emphasized the need for a coordinated industry response, stating that Coinbase was “doing everything we can to support in the current situation.”

“Moments like this call for the industry to work together,” he added.

Tesla chief executive Elon Musk has raised concerns about a potential new threat to the crypto industry, predicting that superintelligent AI systems could eventually steal digital assets to finance their own objectives rather than serve human interests.

Musk shared the warning in an October 30 post on X while commenting on the reported $6.3B security incident involving Binance. He suggested that as artificial intelligence becomes more advanced and autonomous, some systems could seek access to money independently, writing: “Super intelligence agents will at some point do this to gain currency for themselves, not a human.”

Super intelligence agents will at some point do this to gain currency for themselves, not a human

Musk remarks were prompted by a post from crypto commentator Blaney, who described how the attacker behind the reported Binance security incident may have moved funds despite efforts to freeze the stolen assets. As the post noted, stablecoin issuers Tether and Circle froze billions of dollars’ worth of USDT and USDC linked to the incident, but the attacker allegedly obtained Ethereum before the restrictions could fully take effect.

Blaney also claimed the attacker deposited $60 million in USDT into the decentralized lending platform Aave and used it to borrow about $44.6 million in wrapped Ether (WETH). The alleged maneuver illustrates how decentralized finance protocols could potentially be used to move or obtain assets even as centralized issuers work to block suspicious funds.

Musk used the episode to raise a broader concern about the future of artificial intelligence, suggesting that increasingly advanced AI agents could one day carry out similar financial maneuvers autonomously to acquire digital assets for their own purposes rather than for human users.

#5366. Coinbase's October 26 Perpetual Conversion: The Crypto Index the CFTC Waiver Excludes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Coinbase wants six futures contracts to stop expiring on October 26. The CFTC letter it leans on covers five of them by design, and its own footnote points away from the sixth.

The Division of Market Oversight issued Letter 26-29 on October 3, 2026. The CFTC announced it two days later, on October 5, in Release 9308-26. Coverage then focused on the headline that exchanges can now strip expiry dates from perpetual-style index futures. The Merkle flagged the relief's hard October 20 stop on October 19, and outlets like Finance Magnates and FinanceFeeds ran the same window. That coverage, however, predates what Coinbase filed next. This breakdown sets the October 19 filing beside the letter's text, because the two don't line up cleanly.

Meanwhile, the CFTC is working on retail crypto leverage through a different door. As NullTX's earlier breakdown shows, the actual-delivery ANPRM (2026-20888) takes comments until December 14. Perpetuals on registered exchanges skip that process. Instead, they move through staff letters and self-certification.

Coinbase asked for the relief on October 1, and the Division granted it two days later. The letter says staff won't recommend enforcement if a DCM drops expiry dates from existing perpetual-style contracts, as long as the DCM meets eight conditions. First, it must gather feedback from holders of open positions. Next, it must give at least five calendar days' notice and let them close out under the old terms. It must also disclose the risks and change no other material term. Finally, it must file under the CFTC's rules, notify the Division and certify compliance.

Coinbase's Submission #2026-67 then names six contracts: US500, Tech100, Defense10, AI10, China10 and Coin50. It says everything except the expiry stays the same, and that the exchange knows of no substantive opposition. The contract list reached the CFTC by email on October 16.

Letter 26-29 defines its scope by asset class. A footnote shuts out any perpetual-style contract referencing something other than a broad-based security index. Coin50, by contrast, follows the Coinbase 50 Index, and Rule 1148 in the filing itself calls it a futures contract based on a cryptocurrency. In other words, the letter's scope and Coin50's own rule text point in opposite directions.

Crypto contracts did have their own relief. Letter 26-19, issued June 12 to Bitnomial and Coinbase Derivatives, covered digital commodities only and carried the same eight conditions. Even so, it says its positions expire on June 30, 2026. It rests on the Commission's May 29 order and its perpetuals policy statement.

Letter 26-29 sets October 20, 2026 as the day its no-action positions expire. It doesn't say whether implementation itself must happen by then, or only the notice and filing. Coinbase filed on October 19, one day early, but picked October 26 to go live. That choice matters. Ten business days from October 19 lands on November 2, and Coinbase specifically asked to skip that wait. As a result, going live on October 26 depends on the relief still applying.

Without relief, the Division's own words make the path clear. Letter 26-19 says certifications that remove expiry dates will generally draw a stay under Regulation 40.6(c). A stay then gives the Commission another 90 days to review and opens a 30-day public comment period.

Neither side has explained the gap. Searches of news coverage and official channels turned up no statement from Coinbase or the CFTC on whether Coin50 sits inside Letter 26-29, on what authority covers it after October 20, or on why the filing's October 26 date falls after the letter's expiry. We also found no CFTC stay notice and no extension or amendment of Letter 26-29. Likewise, the Coinbase posts we found cover other perpetual launches, not this conversion.

That silence doesn't mean a problem exists. Coinbase may be relying on authority the documents don't mention, and the CFTC may read the letter's dates differently than we do. Still, the paper trail shows a crypto-based contract sitting under relief written for stock indexes, with a start date that falls after that relief expires.

Three developments would settle it: a CFTC stay notice, a new or amended staff letter, or a clarification from Coinbase Derivatives.

Whichever arrives first tells us whether the first U.S.-listed crypto index perpetual goes live on schedule or lands in a 90-day review.

The criticism further escalated when Lagarde said in May 2022 that cryptocurrencies are worth virtually nothing.

"My very humble assessment is that it is worth nothing," Lagarde said during an interview on Dutch television.

Lagarde stated that cryptocurrencies do not have underlying assets that would give investors a solid anchor of safety.

She also warned about inexperienced retail investors risking their savings in speculative crypto investments.

The ECB president also shared that one of her sons had made investments in cryptocurrencies despite her warnings.

In November 2023, she admitted that one of her sons had lost nearly all the money he invested in cryptocurrencies after he didn't heed her advice.

In January 2025, Lagarde emphatically ruled out the option of including Bitcoin in the reserves of European central banks.

#5361. Sprout Ends at Block 3,543,405: What the ZIPs Say About ZEC in Orchard and Sapling

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Zcash has three older shielded pools, and only one of them has a shutdown date. On November 5, NU7 will make the 22,263 ZEC left in Sprout unspendable.

The 346,000 ZEC still in Orchard and the 420,000 ZEC in Sapling face no deadline at all.

But the Zcash specifications include one conditional warning that covers all three pools, and it has been widely misquoted. Let's go through the ZIPs to set out exactly what each document says about each pool, and what it doesn't.

Together, the three older pools hold about 788,000 ZEC. Any full node reports these balances directly through the valuePools field of its getblockchaininfo RPC, so anyone running a node can check them.

The three pools are on very different paths. Sprout has a fixed end. Orchard is closed to new deposits, but no spec sets a closing date. Sapling remains a supported pool.

Sprout's end has been planned for years. ZIP 211, written in 2019, stopped new value from entering Sprout. It described that as "a step toward being able to remove the Sprout shielded protocol."

ZIP 2003 takes the final step. It doesn't target Sprout directly. Instead, it bans an entire transaction format: from NU7 onward, "the transaction version number MUST be 5 or 6." Sprout transfers can only be written as version 4 transactions, so Sprout funds can no longer be spent.

ZIP 259, the NU7 deployment spec, sets the activation height at block 3,543,405 on mainnet. It states the result directly: "funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable."

The wording matters. ZIP 2003 says it does not "unissue, burn, or otherwise make Sprout funds permanently unavailable." The coins stay counted in Zcash's issued supply, and the ZIP leaves open "the theoretical possibility of re-enabling v4 transactions, or of adding another facility to retrieve these funds." It also cautions that this "may never be re-enabled."

Recovering Sprout funds was already hard before the deadline. According to ZIP 2003, the retirement of zcashd just before NU6.3 "removed the only maintained software that still provided wallet functionality for Sprout." The pool has barely changed in the last few weeks: the widely reported figure of 22,309 ZEC has fallen only to 22,263, so about 46 ZEC has moved out since.

Orchard's situation is newer and more unusual. ZIP 258 activated NU6.3 at block 3,428,143 and sealed Orchard after a soundness vulnerability was found and fixed. Since then, the consensus rules have enforced three restrictions:

ZIP 229 explains why: Orchard held "a substantial portion of ZEC" when the vulnerability was fixed, so moving those funds to a fresh pool was meant to restore confidence in Zcash's total supply.

The migration has largely worked. ZecStats counts 3,278,499 ZEC moved out of Orchard, about 90.5% of what was in the pool at NU6.3. That leaves about 346,000 ZEC, roughly 2% of the circulating supply.

Sapling has the fewest restrictions of the three. Version 6 transactions support it as one of the "supported shielded pools," alongside Orchard and Ironwood, and none of the NU6.3 or NU7 ZIPs restricts it.

There's one catch for Sapling users that many people are missing. ZIP 259 says the version 4 ban covers "all version 4 transactions, including transparent-only and Sapling transactions, not only Sprout transfers." Sapling funds stay spendable after NU7, but only through version 5 or version 6 transactions. Wallets still building version 4 transactions need to switch before the upgrade. Pending or offline-signed version 4 transactions won't confirm afterward, and "re-signing alone cannot make a version 4 transaction valid."

The sentence behind the "inaccessible funds" headlines appears in ZIP 2005, "Ironwood Quantum Recoverability," and is repeated in ZIP 229:

"Recovery would not be possible for funds still in the Sprout, Sapling, or Orchard pools; all such funds would be inaccessible after their respective protocols are disabled."

The sentence before it explains the context. Zcash's existing shielded protocols depend on discrete logarithms being hard to compute. If an attacker, using a quantum computer or another method, could break that, the protocols might have to be disabled "to prevent such attacks." Only funds in Ironwood would be recoverable, through a recovery protocol designed to stay secure against quantum attacks.

So this is a contingency, not a schedule. It describes what would happen to funds in the older pools if a future cryptographic emergency forced Zcash to shut them down. No ZIP proposes doing that on any date. The practical advice behind it is plain: funds in Sprout, Sapling or Orchard "should be migrated to the Ironwood pool" to be covered by recovery.

The software is ready. The Zcash Foundation released Zebra 7.0.0 on October 22. Its changelog says it "supports the NU7 network upgrade on Mainnet, which activates at height 3,543,405." The release moves Zebra's database from format v28 to v29. Zebra 6.x can't read the new format, so the Foundation recommends backing up the old state first. The zcashd compatibility sidecar must also be updated to zebra-compat-v1.3.0. Earlier builds can't follow mainnet past NU7.

This upgrade carries more risk than usual. ZIP 259 waives Zcash's usual rule that old software must shut itself down before an upgrade. The spec warns that "operators of unsupported software may therefore remain online at activation and follow a pre-NU7 consensus branch."

For holders, the guidance from each pool's spec comes down to this:

On November 5, Sprout closes. The 766,000 ZEC in Sapling and Orchard face no deadline, but the specs still recommend moving it to Ironwood.

#5360. Polygon Targets Solana’s $5.76T Stablecoin Market With New Payments Integration

Polygon Network is partnering with Solana on its Open Money Stack, which connects bank accounts, crypto wallets, and other services. This follows a string of recent blockchain projects, including adding Tron support and acquiring Coinme.

Polygon Labs is expanding the Open Money Stack’s suite to cater to more networks recording huge user activity. The offering on Solana will let builders accept funding directly from bank accounts, handle payouts, and other multiple crypto services.

Stablecoin demand topped the reasons for the expansion to Solana and other networks. Earlier this month, it integrated on Tron, still based on stablecoin and user activity.

Both networks posted huge numbers this year, capturing a huge chunk of institutional and retail demand. Tron recorded $6.94 trillion worth of stablecoin transfers while Solana saw $5.76 trillion between January and October alone.

“As that activity grows, connecting Solana to bank accounts, wallets and global payout networks allows businesses to deliver stablecoin payments to more customers and markets.” Vibhu Norby, the chief product officer of the Solana Foundation, added.

These assets are growing in popularity because of institutional demand for digital asset products in the same period. Largely, stablecoins are seen as gateway or bridge assets that corporate holders use to gain exposure to other assets.

Stablecoins are the go-to coins before investors make a foray into other crypto like BTC, XRP, SOL, etc because they are tied to the dollar and lower risk. Also, most products lean towards users integrating stablecoins and then gaining decentralized finance (DeFi) exposure with these assets.

According to most users, this adds to the excitement of traditional firms already exploring stablecoin infrastructure. Banks moved on these assets to lower the cost of cross-border payments and improve processing speed.

As expected, volumes soared to new all-time highs on the back of fresh capital. However, regulators flagged instances of the asset class being deployed in illicit transactions, calling for tighter regulations. Generally, laws have become more positive, driving investment, though scrutiny and enforcement rose.

Marc Boiron, Polygon Lab’s CEO, explained that wide adoption and diversity paved the way for new integrations. “We hear from businesses that their customers and payment activity are already spread across networks and that they don’t want to force a chain choice or stitch together a bank provider, wallet, routing service and payout partner for each one.”

#5359. Bitcoin Settles Its $10.9 Billion Options Expiry Right on Max Pain After the Binance Hack

Bitcoin settled Friday’s $10.92 billion Deribit options expiry at $78,119, almost exactly on the $78,000 max pain level, after the $6.36 billion Binance hack knocked it from $80,850 to a $76,500 low overnight.

That low touched BTC’s 200-day EMA, the long-term trend line, to within $32. BTC trades at $77,620, down 3.2% in 24 hours, and the Fear & Greed Index fell from 51 to 30 in a day.

With about a third of Deribit’s open interest now gone, the options market is lighter than it has been all month. The next large date is November 27, when $3.55 billion expires with max pain at $80,000.

Coinbase Premium hit a 4-year low.The last time it was this low was in Nov 2022, right after the FTX collapse, when BTC bottomed.Market sentiment is bearish enough to be bullish, imo. pic.twitter.com/jab4bk1GIX

Discover: Bitcoin Braces for a $10.9 Billion Options Expiry With Max Pain at $78,000, Two Days After the Fed’s Split Hold: Can BTC Hold $79,000?

The drop came in two legs. BTC opened the 20:00 UTC hour on Thursday at $80,850 and hit $78,297 within minutes as news of the Binance breach spread, a 3.2% fall. It bounced, then slid again after 23:00 UTC and printed its $76,500 low just after 02:00 UTC on Friday, 5.4% below where the hour began.

Forced selling did much of the work. CoinGlass data showed $1.55 billion of crypto positions liquidated in 24 hours, 83.6% of them longs, with $501.6 million in BTC alone.

Smaller accounts bought the dip: the share of OKX accounts that are long jumped as the price fell, and open interest rose by about $210 million into the low. Funding on OKX’s BTC perpetual stayed positive throughout, so longs are still paying shorts.

Implied volatility told a more cautious story. Deribit’s DVOL index, which tracks the 30-day volatility options traders are pricing in, jumped from 37 before the hack to 42 just before midnight UTC and has only eased back to 38.7.

About 135,000 BTC of options expired on Deribit at 08:00 UTC on Friday, the last Friday of the month, when monthly contracts settle. Max pain, the strike where the most options expire worthless, sat at $78,000. Deribit settled the contracts at $78,119.01.

The book was heavily tilted toward calls. Deribit data reported before the expiry put the put/call ratio at 0.53, close to two calls for every put. With BTC settling just above $78,000, most of those calls, bets that BTC would be higher by the end of October, expired worthless.

Once the expiry cleared, Deribit’s BTC options open interest stood at 285,073 BTC, or about $22.1 billion, as of 11:17 UTC.

BTC options notional by Deribit expiry as of 11:17 UTC on October 30, 2026. Source: Deribit.

Max pain isn’t a forecast; BTC often settles far from it. But the November levels frame the range traders are betting on: puts clustered at $74,000 to $76,000, right around the 200-day EMA, and calls stacked from $90,000 up.

One more sign of caution: in the 24 hours to 11:17 UTC on Friday, Deribit traders bought 1.63 BTC of puts for every BTC of calls, the reverse of the call-heavy book that just expired.

On the daily chart since early August, BTC is back where it spent most of September: between its 200-day EMA at $76,468 and its 50-day EMA at $80,593. Friday’s low wick stopped $32 above the 200-day line, which BTC has closed above every day since its late-August breakout.

August 2 to October 30, 2026: BTCUSDT 1D chart. Source: Binance.

The levels line up with the options book:

BTC has tested this 200-day zone before. In mid-September, it dipped to $74,968, held, and ran to $87,395 within a week. Friday’s buyers are betting on the same bounce, as the OKX long/short ratio shows.

Discover: Bitcoin Swings Less Than Coinbase and Oracle, Yet Crypto Stocks Move Up to 2.4 Times as Hard: Why?

For Bitcoin, the next test is Binance itself. If withdrawals reopen smoothly within the promised 48 hours, the call-heavy positioning that just expired worthless could rebuild toward the $90,000 strikes. If they don’t, the puts at $74,000 to $76,000 are where traders have already placed their bets.

#5358. Solana Validator Admission Ticket: Who Fell Short After Alpenglow, and How Marinade Responded

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

StakeThat +MEV went into one of Solana's first Alpenglow epochs with about 137,000 SOL staked with it and 0.8169 SOL in its vote account. The new admission ticket required 0.8198 SOL. It was 0.003 SOL short.

That's the first post-activation picture of Solana's Validator Admission Ticket. Most stake made it through without trouble, but a small group of validators keeps dropping in and out, often by amounts smaller than a typical transaction fee. At least one large stake program changed its delegation code hours before activation so its stake wouldn't stay with those validators. Marinade's published validator snapshots for epochs 1063 to 1067 show who fell short and what happened next.

According to Solana's BLS Pubkey and VAT page, Alpenglow has been active on mainnet since epoch 1064, which began around 13:36 UTC on October 21. From then on, each validator's vote account pays a 0.8 SOL Validator Admission Ticket at the start of every epoch. The fee is burned, and it pays for the following epoch. The first charge, at the start of epoch 1064, covered epoch 1065.

The rules are strict. If the fee can't be paid, Solana's page says, "your validator does not vote or produce blocks in the next epoch." Validators without a registered BLS key, or outside the top 2,000 by stake, are also excluded. Delegators to an excluded validator earn no inflation rewards for that epoch. The page also stresses that the balance "has to stay funded, not be funded once."

The vote account also has to stay above its rent-exempt minimum. In Marinade's data, the full requirement works out to 0.8197612 SOL.

Marinade publishes the inputs to its stake auction every epoch in a public pipeline repository. The input data checks whether each validator's vote account holds enough to cover the next epoch's ticket. Each snapshot covers about 670 validators and roughly 438 million SOL of stake.

Before activation, in the epoch 1063 snapshot, 33 validators holding 7.63 million SOL, or 1.74% of stake, were below the ticket balance. Once Alpenglow went live, that number fell quickly: 15 validators with 1.55 million SOL (0.35%) in epoch 1064, then 19 with 1.15 million (0.26%) in epoch 1065, the first epoch the ticket actually paid for. By epoch 1066 it was 13 validators with 790,000 SOL (0.18%), and by epoch 1067 just 8 with 710,000 SOL (0.16%).

The epoch 1063 count matches a figure in Marinade's own code history. A commit on October 21 notes that its new gate "refuses the 33 validators with vat_eligible false" in the 1063 snapshot.

The biggest pre-activation gaps were fixed in time. An unnamed validator with 2.05 million SOL of stake, Temporal Emerald with 1.23 million and Bitget Wallet with 593,000 were all below the ticket balance in epoch 1063. All three had topped up by the next snapshot. Of the 33 flagged before activation, 25 had recovered by epoch 1064.

So the fee didn't remove a large share of stake. The balance check affected less than 2% of stake at its peak, and about 0.16% by epoch 1067.

The validators that did fall short show a pattern: many of them nearly had enough.

Because the ticket is charged every epoch, a validator that tops up just enough to pass once will fail again an epoch later unless it adds more. Between epochs 1064 and 1067, between 3 and 11 validators fell below the threshold each epoch, while a similar number recovered.

The shortfalls also cut across setups. Every validator flagged in epoch 1067 runs either Agave 4.3.x, the client release the migration required, or the latest Firedancer build. Software readiness wasn't the issue. Keeping the balance funded was.

Solana offers a fix: routing block revenue to the vote account through solana vote-update-commission-collector. That keeps the account funded automatically, though the change takes two epochs to apply.

The bigger story is how stake programs reacted. Marinade, one of Solana's largest delegation programs, changed its auction code in pull request #153, merged at about 06:47 UTC on October 21, roughly seven hours before Alpenglow activated.

The change adds a new disqualifying condition, vatIneligible. A validator whose vat_eligible flag is false "gets no SAM and no backstop stake," because "Agave then pays its stakers no inflation rewards for the epoch." A null value never disqualifies a validator. The check currently tests only the SIMD-0357 balance, not BLS key registration.

The first version applied the rule only in Alpenglow epochs. Marinade's developers then caught a timing problem. Agave starts charging the ticket at the 1063-to-1064 boundary, and "a stake move made in epoch E takes effect in E+1," so the original rule "left Marinade stake on refused validators for epochs 1064 and 1065." The merged version refuses ineligible validators in every epoch.

The snapshots confirm it worked. In the epoch 1064 snapshot, 192,762 SOL of Marinade stake sat on ineligible validators, nearly all of it on one unnamed validator. By epoch 1065, that had dropped to 2,407 SOL, and by epoch 1066 to 10 SOL. A later commit gives the rule its own label and call to action in Marinade's interface, so operators can see why they've been excluded.

Marinade, in short, turned a protocol fee into a delegation rule of its own. A validator that misses one ticket loses an epoch of rewards, and it also loses Marinade stake until its balance recovers.

Before activation, Solana Compass reported that a community tracker flagged 45% of stake as not ready two days ahead of epoch 1064, mostly validators on Agave 4.3.0 and 4.3.1. The following day, that had dropped to 20.3%.

Marinade's snapshots show the software gap closing much as those warnings suggested it needed to. Stake on Agave 4.3.0 and 4.3.1 fell from 6.56% in epoch 1063 to 0.08% by epoch 1067. Firedancer operators, who had to switch to Agave for the migration, dropped from 11.0% of stake to 5.9% in epoch 1064. They then came back strongly, reaching 17.2% by epoch 1067, well above their pre-migration share.

The large readiness gap was about software and keys, and it was mostly closed by the time it mattered. The fee gap was always small.

For most delegators, nothing changed: more than 99.8% of stake sits with validators that keep their tickets paid. For those delegated to the few that don't, the cost is clear: no inflation rewards for that epoch, and in Marinade's case, stake moved elsewhere.

The protocol sets one requirement: 0.8 SOL in the vote account every epoch. Stake programs are now adding their own rules on top, starting with Marinade's. Validators that keep running near the threshold will keep losing epochs of rewards, and possibly delegations, until they keep a buffer or automate funding.

#5355. CoinDepo Revises Earn Rates to Reflect Asset Economics and Deployment Horizons

All reviews, research, news and assessments of any kind on The Tokenist are compiled using a strict editorial review process by our editorial team. Neither our writers nor our editors receive direct compensation of any kind to publish information on tokenist.com. Our company, Tokenist Media LLC, is community supported and may receive a small commission when you purchase products or services through links on our website. Click here for a full list of our partners and an in-depth explanation on how we get paid.

CoinDepo is introducing revised Earn rates effective November 8, 2026. The changes connect the economics of each supported asset with the practical requirements of managing client capital across different account lengths.

Client deposits are placed into a diversified portfolio whose primary focus is lending. At the close of the second quarter of 2026, overcollateralized crypto lending represented 37% of deployed capital and microcredit programs represented 24%. Remaining allocations covered liquidity pools, real-world and private-market investments, stablecoin yield strategies, and market-neutral trading.

Income produced by these activities funds the interest paid to users and also covers operating costs and liquidity needs. The resulting APRs therefore align with the broader economics of operating the CoinDepo platform.

Daily APRs will decline for every asset listed in CoinDepo’s 30-asset update table. EURC is handled separately and keeps its 10% Daily APR. USDT and USDC Daily APRs will adjust from 17% to 15% while their Annual APRs change from 23% to 22%. BTC and ETH Daily APRs move from 12% to 11%, with Annual APR remaining at 18%.

Across the 30 assets, the difference between Daily and Annual rates expands from six percentage points to seven. The adjustments will also be asset-specific as well as period-specific; the Annual APR for Filecoin (FIL), for instance, will be changed from 18% to 12%.

Short-term funds require the platform to retain greater flexibility so that withdrawals can be met without delay. A more predictable funding horizon simplifies the planning of capital allocation and the matching of funds with available lending and investment opportunities. The wider gap between Daily and Annual APRs places greater weight on that planning advantage. Daily accounts continue to be offered for users who place priority on ready access to their funds.

CoinDepo’s open Monthly, Quarterly, Semi-Annual and Annual Interest Accounts will keep their current APR through the remainder of the active term. Revised rates apply only to accounts that are newly opened or renewed after the effective date. The complete before-and-after comparison appears in the platform’s Earn rate update, together with the business disclosures that describe the activities supporting client interest.

CoinDepo is a centralized digital asset platform that provides crypto interest accounts and portfolio-backed borrowing services.

#5354. Polymarket Hit by Massive Hack

A massive security breach has reportedly seen nearly 1,000 accounts on the crypto-based prediction market Polymarket drained, with the attack leading to losses of more than $2.6M.

Blockchain analyst Conor Grogan revealed that a total of 995 accounts were hit by the attack, resulting in losses of roughly $2.65 million.

Polymarket has seen 995 accounts drained by a hacker, for $2,654,211.42. Largest losses were 341k and 307k Hacker has converted all funds to POL (most likely to avoid freezing) https://t.co/PjT2QhgBSa

The two biggest losses detected by Grogan were $341K and $307K.

Moreover, the analyst also revealed that the attacker has converted all stolen funds into Polygon's native token (POL). This move might have been made to avoid having the funds frozen.

"If you are a @Polymarket user lock your account. I just got drained $800,000," a trader warned via X.

The trader also claimed that a friend lost another $600K and warned users not to interact with the website.

As noted by blockchain investigator StarPlatinum, the attacker stole roughly $2.68M in just one hour.

The data shows that at about 17:05 UTC, an empty wallet began receiving funds.

At 17:25 UTC, the wallet had amassed roughly $412K.

However, the figure jumped to $2.02M at 17:50 UTC and reached roughly $2.68M at 18:05 UTC.

In total, the attacker has amassed some 28.6M POL tokens, as noted.

So far, it appears that the attack might have occurred due to a hack of a third-party JavaScript component that was embedded in the Polymarket website.

It's not the first time that the popular prediction market has faced a massive hack leading to a multimillion-dollar security breach.

We've identified & fixed an issue impacting our international platform, Polymarket⁠.com. One of our 3rd party providers was compromised, and we have referred this to relevant law enforcement. Anyone who has been impacted will be made whole. Out of an abundance of caution, we have temporarily halted trading & are working to bring the platform back online.

In June, Polymarket also faced a similar hack. The attack happened when hackers compromised a third-party vendor and injected malicious JavaScript into the frontend of Polymarket.

In total, some $2.94 million was stolen from at least 11 wallets.

Now, Polymarket has reportedly confirmed that the security breach occurred due to a hack of a third-party service provider.

The company also vowed to make every affected user whole. In other words, users who suffered losses due to the attack will be compensated.

#5353. Hackers Target Crypto Users With Fake ChatGPT and Claude Apps

Cybercriminals have been using the hype surrounding artificial intelligence (AI) technologies to distribute cryptocurrency mining malware through fake desktop apps that mimic popular AI tools like ChatGPT and Claude.

In a recent report, cybersecurity vendor Check Point Research (CPR) said threat actors have been setting up fake GitHub repositories to advertise fake AI apps like GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus, among others.

The hackers have even set up dedicated GitHub.io sites that promote their fake AI apps and trick victims into downloading malicious files.

According to the CPR researchers, the attackers are using search engine optimization (SEO) manipulation to get their malicious sites to rank high on Google.

One of the most worrisome aspects of the campaign is how the attackers use legitimate software components from OpenAI and Anthropic to mask malicious activity.

The malicious ZIP archives that victims can download feature legitimate digitally signed executable files. These legitimate executables are bundled with malicious DLLs.

Once victims run the seemingly legitimate application, the malicious DLL gets loaded without their knowledge, thanks to the DLL sideloading technique.

This makes it very hard for victims to spot the attack since the malware relies on legitimate software to run its code.

At the end of the day, the attack leads to the installation of XMRig, a cryptocurrency miner that quietly uses the victims' resources to mine digital assets for the attackers.

Interestingly, the malware can also stop mining whenever it senses user activity so that it can evade detection.

In addition, CPR researchers discovered that the malware includes several techniques to make security investigations harder.

For example, it can pause execution for a very long time if it senses that it is not running under the expected executable file.

It also checks the keyboard language setting on a computer before going ahead with the infection.

The first GitHub repository for the campaign showed up in July 2026, and malicious downloads started popping up at the end of August.

At the moment, the payload is a cryptocurrency miner, but researchers have warned that YobaLoader can potentially be used to deploy other types of malware.

#5352. Cosmos Hub Approves Gaia v29 With 99.41% Support Ahead of October 28th Upgrade

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Proposal #1059 passed with 49.59% turnout as the chain counts down now to block 33,618,500 on October 28th, where validators are told to run the security-patched v29.0.1 binary, not the version named in the proposal.

The Cosmos Hub's latest upgrade drew almost no opposition. About 168.5 million ATOM voted on Proposal #1059, and only 2,335 ATOM voted No. Under that one-sided result is an unusual change: the Hub's stakers voted to remove the governance route that earlier generations of Cosmos proposals used to change the chain's own settings.

Proposal #1059 schedules the upgrade of the Cosmos Hub to Gaia v29.0.0. It finished voting on October 27 at 12:00 UTC with a PASSED result. The vote approves the upgrade, but the software has not run yet. The chain still has to reach the upgrade height, halt, and restart on the new binary. Until that happens, Gaia v29 is approved but not yet live.

On-chain records show 49.59% of staked ATOM voted, against a 40% quorum requirement. Yes took 99.41% of the vote, or 167,514,965 ATOM. No With Veto took 0.58% (982,855 ATOM), Abstain took 0.01% (14,360 ATOM), and No rounds to 0.00% (2,335 ATOM).

The veto share is the main number to watch in a Cosmos governance vote, because a large enough veto rejects a proposal even if Yes wins. At 0.58%, the veto bloc was far too small to matter. That fits the proposal's nature. It is a maintenance release that removes deprecated code and updates dependencies, and it has no economic or political stakes.

The forum discussion covered one governance point: a delegator's own vote overrides their validator's vote. A few large validators did not decide the result on their own. Delegators could have overridden them, and very few chose to vote differently.

The proposal names v29.0.0, but operators are not supposed to run that build at the upgrade height. On October 23, three days into voting, the Gaia team tagged v29.0.1 and updated the official forum post to recommend it.

The patch changes only one thing: it rebuilds Gaia with Go 1.26.10 instead of Go 1.26.7. That picks up the Go security fix tracked as CVE-2026-111943 (GO-2026-6809). The project's upgrade notes call v29.0.1 a non-state-breaking patch release, so it computes the same chain state as v29.0.0. Nodes that already installed v29.0.0 can switch at any time by replacing the binary and restarting.

Operators using Cosmovisor need to know one detail. The on-chain upgrade name stays v29.0.0, so the v29.0.1 binary still goes into the upgrades/v29.0.0/bin/ directory. If a validator names the folder after the patch version, Cosmovisor will not find the binary when the chain halts. The project's sample service configuration has automatic binary download turned off, which means each operator has to put the correct binary in place before the halt.

Gaia v29 removes the x/params module from the Cosmos Hub. That module is the original, centralized store for parameters, and it backed the legacy ParameterChangeProposal governance route. The release changelog lists the change under API-breaking changes: "The legacy ParameterChangeProposal governance route and cosmos.params.v1beta1.Query service are no longer available."

In practice, governance has already moved on. Each module now owns its parameters, and changes go through that module's own governance message. The legacy route remained as a fallback, and v29 removes it. The rate-limiting module was the last part of the Hub still wired to the old params subspace. In v29 it no longer depends on it.

The forum Q&A states who is affected. RPC providers, wallets, explorers, and governance dashboards should check whether they still call the params v1beta1 query service or create legacy parameter-change proposals. After the upgrade, those calls will fail on the Hub. For most users nothing changes. The proposal requires no token migration, and balances, delegations, and IBC assets are unaffected.

The second API-breaking item affects multisig accounts specifically. Gaia v29 moves the Hub from Cosmos SDK v0.53.4 to v0.53.8, and the changelog warns: "As of cosmos-sdk v0.53.8, --gas auto gas simulation is broken for multisig senders. Multisig transactions must specify a fixed --gas value until this is fixed upstream."

This matters in practice. The Hub's weekly update of October 22 said the problem applies to the Community Pool migration multisig. That multisig is handling a USDC.n migration spend that was moving toward an on-chain proposal during the same week. Treasury signers, custody desks, and DAO operators who build transactions with --gas auto will need to set gas by hand until the upstream SDK is fixed.

The same release also brings CometBFT from 0.38.23 to 0.38.25, the IBC rate-limiting middleware from 10.1.0 to 10.7.0, and runc from 1.2.8 to 1.3.6. It also moves the build toolchain from Go 1.25 to Go 1.26.

The upgrade handler, the code that runs once at the upgrade height, does more cleanup than the proposal summary describes. It first deletes everything in the deprecated provider store, the state left over from the Hub's time as an Interchain Security provider. Next it wipes the legacy x/params store. Last, it removes a receipt left behind by the earlier v28.3.1 balance migration.

The code also shows how cautious the Gaia team is about the upgrade. The stores stay mounted, and their contents are cleared as ordinary state changes. Unmounting them entirely could cause version-mismatch errors when nodes load the chain from disk. Gaia v29 has also run on the Hub's provider testnet since October 13, about two weeks before mainnet.

At 15:32 UTC on October 27, Mintscan showed block 33,618,500 as "not yet created". The chain was at block 33,604,199, with 14,301 blocks to go. At the recent average block time of 5.722 seconds, the Mintscan countdown for block 33,618,500 estimated the height for about 14:16 UTC on October 28. The forum's original estimate was 13:50 UTC. The real time depends on how fast blocks are produced over the next day.

When the chain reaches that height, block production stops. It restarts only after validators holding more than two-thirds of voting power are back online on the new binary. That makes the vote result only half the story. The other half is whether validators show up on v29.0.1 promptly, so that the halt lasts minutes rather than hours.
