#5309. Exchange Ledgers in the Middle as CFTC and SEC Diverge on What “Delivery” Means

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

A customer buys a token on a U.S. exchange and the app shows the balance. Under the CFTC's December 14 framework, nothing has been delivered yet.

Under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all. An October 27 comment letter asks the two agencies to settle on one answer.

Open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available. To the customer, the asset is theirs. To the exchange's database, it's a row in an internal ledger. To federal regulators, that row is now being judged by two different tests that don't agree on what it means.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has opened an advance notice of proposed rulemaking on what it calls Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions (CTX) and Regulation Crypto Asset Markets (CAM). It sets out the agency's first formal view of "actual delivery" for crypto since it withdrew its 2020 guidance last December. Comments close on December 14.

The Securities and Exchange Commission's Regulation Crypto Assets proposal takes a different view of the same moment. Then, on October 27, a comment letter on the SEC's file raised the gap directly. It described the situation as "two conflicting definitions of the same physical facts" and asked the agencies to "please coordinate the definitions."

Delivery matters because it decides which rulebook applies.

For the CFTC, the answer comes from Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act. A leveraged, margined or financed retail commodity trade is treated like a futures contract unless "actual delivery" happens within 28 days. If delivery happens in time, the trade falls outside futures rules. If it doesn't, the exchange is effectively running a futures venue.

For the SEC, the question is whether a token is still part of an investment contract. Under the August proposal, a covered investment contract ends when the issuer has finished or permanently stopped its essential managerial efforts and files a Form TR transition report. Whether the buyer has received the token is not part of that test.

So one agency treats delivery as the deciding question, and the other barely considers it.

The CFTC's position is still preliminary, but it is detailed. Published in the Federal Register on October 13, the notice relies on the Monex case standard: actual delivery requires "the transfer of some meaningful degree of possession or control."

For crypto, the agency suggests that possession and control "may require possession of the credentials (e.g., private key(s))." It takes three positions that matter most to exchanges:

The agency is also asking whether control has to be exclusive, whether delivery can happen while a lien or security interest is outstanding, and how financing offered in an exchange's standard account documents affects whether a trade is covered at all.

The SEC's proposal, released on August 18, deals with a different question. It creates offering exemptions, including a $5 million startup exemption over four years, and a safe harbor for when a crypto asset's investment contract ends. Neither depends on where the token sits.

Under the proposal, a token held in a customer's self-custody wallet and a token recorded on an exchange's books are treated the same way. In both cases, the investment contract question depends on the issuer's managerial efforts and its filings.

That is the gap the October 27 letter tries to close. Its author, who describes themselves as a fintech founder designing a consumer platform, argues that "where the customer holds the private keys or execution is on-chain, with custody evidence, the asset should be treated as delivered and the covered-investment-contract analysis should end there."

Running four common exchange transactions through both frameworks shows where the tests split.

Trade one: a fully paid purchase left on the exchange.

Trade two: the same purchase withdrawn to a self-custody wallet on day three.

Trade three: a margined purchase kept on the exchange's ledger for 30 days.

Trade four: an on-chain swap that settles directly into the user's wallet.

The pattern is consistent. Self-custody is the only position that clearly counts as delivery under the CFTC's view and also ends the analysis under the letter's proposed SEC fix. Everything left on an exchange's internal ledger stays in an unclear position. The CFTC treats it as undelivered and the SEC's text doesn't address it.

The letter was filed on October 27, a week after the SEC's October 20 comment deadline. It is anonymous and brief, but its main concern is practical. If the definitions stay separate, it warns, founders will have to design products around whichever rule is stricter.

It is the only filing on either docket so far that sets the two definitions side by side.

The CFTC process is still at the advance-notice stage, so a formal proposal will follow. For U.S. platforms, though, the direction is clear. Under the CFTC's preliminary reading, an exchange that keeps customer assets in internal ledger accounts has not delivered them. If that exchange also offers margin or financing, it is on track to be treated as a futures venue.

The SEC's final rule could adopt the letter's custody-based approach or keep delivery out of its analysis entirely. Until one of those happens, the same ledger entry can be undelivered for one regulator and irrelevant for the other.

Exchanges and their customers have until December 14 to say which definition should prevail. The real decision is whether "delivered" ends up meaning the same thing at both agencies.

#5308. Bitcoin Midterm Election Pattern: Will BTC Repeat Its Post-Election Rally?

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin could be approaching another major historical turning point as Americans prepare to vote in the 2026 midterm election. The crypto market has struggled through a difficult October, but previous midterm elections delivered surprisingly strong returns over the following year.

Bitcoin gained an average of 53.7% during the 12 months after the 2014, 2018, and 2022 midterms. With BTC trading at the $78,000 level ahead of the November 3 vote, we are watching to see if history offers another bullish signal.

Bitcoin and its midterm election pattern have coincided with major market transitions. However, the short-term aftermath was often painful and is leaving us with an important question. Could 2026 finally deliver a smoother recovery?

Bitcoin’s performance following the previous three U.S. midterm elections paints a good picture for long-term holders. BTC gained 24.1% during the year following the 2014 election. BTC then advanced 43.4% after the 2018 midterms and 92% following the 2022 vote.

The immediate aftermath also tells a different story. Bitcoin fell 27.5% during the 90 days following the 2014 election and plunged 46.5% after the 2018 vote. The 2022 election delivered a more favorable 90-day return of 22.6%.

These contrasting outcomes show that the Bitcoin midterm election pattern is more compelling over longer periods, not in the short term.

Now, the 2026 election arrives during a different phase of Bitcoin’s market cycle. Previous midterm elections occurred during years when Bitcoin was still approaching major cycle lows. In 2014 and 2018, the crypto market continued falling after Election Day before eventually recovering. The 2022 election also preceded another decline, partly driven by the FTX collapse.

Bitcoin’s current setup could be different if the June low near $57,803 ultimately holds. BTC has already rebounded from that level, potentially placing the market in an early recovery phase heading into the midterms.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Bitcoin’s relationship with U.S. politics has become increasingly important as Washington shapes the regulatory future of digital assets. From presidential elections to congressional battles, political decisions can influence investor sentiment, institutional demand, and the direction of the crypto market.

The 2024 election offered a clear example, with BTC surging to record highs as Donald Trump’s victory fueled expectations of a more crypto-friendly administration. Bitcoin climbed above $75,000 immediately after the result and continued rallying toward $100,000 in the following weeks.

Regulatory policy is one of the strongest links between Bitcoin and U.S. politics. Investors closely watch the White House, Congress, the SEC, and the CFTC for decisions that could affect exchanges, ETFs, institutional participation, and crypto businesses.

The stalled CLARITY Act has become a major political battleground, with lawmakers divided over market oversight and ethics provisions. When the Senate failed to advance the bill in September, Bitcoin dropped more than 5%, showing how quickly legislative setbacks can influence market sentiment.

🇺🇸 Treasury Secretary Bessent says Treasury will work with the SEC and CFTC to fill the crypto regulation gaps left by the stalled Clarity Act.He called Congress’s failure to pass the bill a disappointment. pic.twitter.com/8JakMNfFEl

Congressional elections also matter because they determine whether crypto legislation can move forward. The industry has poured $176 million into the 2026 midterm races, backing candidates viewed as favorable to digital assets and seeking influence that can survive beyond the current administration.

Politics can also influence Bitcoin through economic policy. Government spending, tariffs, tax changes, and expectations for Federal Reserve policy can move the dollar, Treasury yields, and investor appetite for risk.

Bitcoin often benefits when markets anticipate easier financial conditions or stronger demand for alternative assets, while rising yields and a stronger dollar can pressure speculative investments. This makes U.S. political developments an increasingly important part of Bitcoin’s market outlook, with election results capable of shifting both regulatory expectations and macroeconomic sentiment.

The Dogecoin community gets a security alert after wallet provider Trezor revealed a suspected hardware implant in its Safe 5 device bought from CryptoBilis.

Dogecoin community member Mishaboar urged users who purchased a Trezor device from CryptoBilis in March this year or later to take immediate precautions, including moving their funds to a completely new wallet with a freshly generated recovery seed.

"If you bought a Trezor from CryptoBilis in March 2026 or later, move your funds to a completely new wallet, with a newly generated recovery seed, as soon as possible," Mishaboar wrote.

If you bought a Trezor from CryptoBilis in March 2026 or later, move your funds to a completely new wallet, with a newly generated recovery seed, as soon as possible. Use a device and wallet you trust to create the new wallet. If your wallet supports an additional passphrase, use it (and remember to write it down in your offline backups). NEVER reuse a recovery seed from a wallet that might have been compromised. Simply resetting the device or importing the same seed into another wallet does NOT make your funds safe. An ELI5: I know this is obvious to many of you, but in my experience some people don't realize that hardware wallets don't actually "contain" their coins. Your coins "live" on the blockchain. Your wallet only holds the keys that allow you to access and spend them. If someone else has a copy of those keys, they can access your funds from anywhere in the world, from any device where those keys are imported. They don't need your physical little device or your phone to access it.

Users are warned never to reuse a recovery seed from a wallet that might have been compromised. Simply resetting the device or importing the same seed into another wallet does not make funds safe either.

Mishaboar highlighted a critical security principle that may not seem obvious to all users: hardware wallets do not actually "contain" coins—the coins "live" on the blockchain. The wallet only holds the keys that allow access to and spending of the coins. If someone obtains these keys, they can access the funds from anywhere in the world on any device where the keys are imported, without needing the physical device or the user's phone.

Mishaboar's warning follows a recent update from Trezor regarding CryptoBilis, in which the company disclosed that it had been alerted through responsible disclosure to a suspected hardware implant in a Trezor Safe 5 device purchased from CryptoBilis in August 2026.

According to Trezor, the reported device has not yet been received for physical examination. However, the company said it considers the report credible enough to notify customers while its security team investigates. No CryptoBilis buyer has reported losing funds to the company so far.

In light of this, affected users are urged to move their funds to a newly created wallet with a new seed as soon as possible. Those who have not yet set up their device should never do so using an existing wallet backup (recovery phrase), nor share this information with anyone.

#5304. Clock Ticking on Zcash’s Sprout Pool: 22,263 ZEC Unmoved Ahead of NU7 Lock

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Daily pool data shows Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped. The last withdrawal was on October 19.

Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.

Most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC. That number is accurate, but it is a single snapshot. It doesn't show whether the people who own those coins are doing anything about the deadline.

We checked the pool every day, and the answer so far is no.

According to ZecStats' daily value-pool records, Sprout has held exactly 22,263.34162335 ZEC since October 19. That is 11 straight days, and more than 12,000 blocks, without a single zatoshi leaving the pool. Our October 25 piece recorded the drop from 22,309 ZEC to 22,263 ZEC. Since then the balance hasn't moved.

ZecStats publishes a daily CSV of every Zcash value pool, using the last block of each UTC day. Its figures follow the valuePools field that a full node returns through the getblockchaininfo call. The archive starts on July 30, 2026, and gives a 92-day picture of the Sprout pool.

Across those 92 days, about 374 ZEC, or 1.65% of the pool, left Sprout. That is an average of roughly 4 ZEC a day. The average hides the real pattern, though: the pool moved on only 15 of the 92 days.

Most of the withdrawals came in a few large transfers in September:

Together with smaller moves on August 31, September 17 and September 19, the 30 days to September 29 saw 310.5 ZEC leave Sprout. That is about 10 ZEC a day.

October was much quieter. Apart from one withdrawal of 46.05 ZEC on October 19, the month's activity was small change:

Since October 19, there has been no movement at all.

At September's pace, about 70 ZEC more would leave before activation. At October's pace, it would be well under 15 ZEC. On the last 11 days' pace, the answer is zero.

The deadline is set in ZIP 259, which defines how the NU7 network upgrade is deployed. It sets the mainnet activation height at 3,543,405.

NU7 does not introduce a new transaction format. Instead, after activation, version 4 transactions become invalid, while versions 5 and 6 remain valid. Sprout's design is the problem. As ZIP 259 puts it: "Because Sprout transfers can only be represented by version 4 transactions, funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable."

The coins would not be destroyed, and NU7 does not change Zcash's supply cap. They would simply be stuck in a pool that no valid transaction can spend from. Today the stranded amount would be 22,263 ZEC, about 0.13% of the roughly 17.01 million ZEC in circulation.

ZIP 259 also skips Zcash's usual three-month gap between the first supporting software release and activation. Operators running unsupported software could stay online and follow a pre-NU7 chain.

As of ZecStats' latest update on October 30 at 13:09 UTC, the chain was at block 3,535,877. That leaves 7,528 blocks until activation.

In October, the network averaged about 1,147 blocks a day, or one roughly every 75.3 seconds. At that rate, block 3,543,405 arrives around 02:00–03:00 UTC on November 6. That is the evening of November 5 in the Americas and the early hours of November 6 in Europe and Africa.

Small changes in block times could move that window by a few hours. Holders who plan to move funds on the final day risk missing the cutoff.

In practice, getting funds out of Sprout means sending a version 4 transaction that moves them into a newer pool before activation. Users need software that can still build Sprout transactions and a synced node or wallet that recognizes their old notes.

The September withdrawals show that some holders are still paying attention. Several were round amounts, such as 99.998 ZEC, which is consistent with someone moving 100 ZEC and paying a fee. The 11-day pause since October 19 suggests something else: most of the remaining 22,263 ZEC may belong to keys that are lost, forgotten or no longer used.

That has been part of the debate about Sprout for years. A pool that has been shrinking slowly since Zcash's early days is now on a fixed timetable. The daily data indicates that most of its remaining balance is not being moved.

Every report that cites "about 22,000 ZEC at risk" is technically correct. The more useful figure for anyone tracking the upgrade is the rate of change, and right now that rate is zero.

The useful thing to watch over the next week is whether the Sprout line in ZecStats' daily data moves again before block 3,543,405. If it doesn't, Zcash will activate NU7 with about 22,263 ZEC permanently locked in its first shielded pool. That would be one of the largest deliberate freezes of user funds by any major blockchain upgrade, and nearly all of it would be coins whose owners did not move them in time.

It's the 18th anniversary of the Bitcoin whitepaper. Today marks the historic date on which its pseudonymous creator Satoshi Nakamoto published the blueprint for the first digital cash.

On Oct. 31, 2008, a nine-page white paper called "Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System" was published, laying out a radical vision for transferring value electronically without the need for conventional financial intermediaries.

Bitcoin supporters, exchanges, and the rest of the crypto community are filling social media platform X with celebratory wishes on the 18th anniversary of Bitcoin's unveiling to the world.

Bitcoin proponent and Strategy Chairman Michael Saylor wrote on X: "Happy Bitcoin white paper day. 18 years."

One of the most salient features of the whitepaper is the fixed supply of Bitcoin at 21 million coins. The pre-determined issuance structure is what makes Bitcoin different from traditional monetary systems, where central authorities can inflate the money supply.

Major U.S. crypto exchange Coinbase highlighted this fact in its X post: "21,000,000. Never more. Happy Bitcoin Whitepaper Day."

21,000,000. Never more. Happy Bitcoin Whitepaper Day. https://t.co/JtKeHtCuSM

"Today marks 18 years since the release of the Bitcoin Whitepaper. A day that changed everything," Coinbase continued.

Stablecoin issuer Tether wrote: "On 31 October 2008, Satoshi published nine pages that explained Bitcoin to the world. Today we're explaining it to everyone else. Two pizzas, 10,000 BTC, 21 million coins, and one key you never share. Everything you need to know, in a comic. Happy 18th birthday, Bitcoin whitepaper."

Crypto platform Uphold wrote: "Nine pages that challenged the entire legacy financial system. Happy Bitcoin Whitepaper Day."

The Bitcoin whitepaper laid the groundwork for the network's launch in January 2009, when Satoshi Nakamoto mined Bitcoin's genesis block and introduced the first units of the cryptocurrency.

When Bitcoin launched on January 3, 2009, it had no market value or official exchange price. Over the years, Bitcoin has evolved from a niche technological experiment into a globally recognized digital asset. Its emergence has influenced the development of thousands of cryptocurrencies, blockchain applications, and decentralized financial systems.

The cryptocurrency now trades at $77,310 and is worth $1.55 trillion, according to CoinMarketCap data.

XRP's burn rate is shooting up toward the end of October, surging 147%. According to data from XRPScan, XRP burned as fees came in at 1,644 on October 30.

The burn activity is a representation of the XRP Ledger's deflationary mechanism, which permanently removes small amounts of XRP from circulation every time transactions are processed on the network.

Some blockchains have scheduled mechanisms to distribute burned tokens, but XRP burns are automatic through transaction fees. Every transaction on the XRP Ledger requires a fee denominated in XRP and that fee is burned.

A total of 14,423,678 XRP, representing 0.014% of its total supply, has been burned so far.

Often referred to as "Uptober" in crypto circles thanks to a track record of outperformance, October might need to shed that nickname given that major cryptocurrencies, including XRP, are down for the month. #5295. Circle Begins CCTP V1 Wind-Down Amid Doc Mismatch

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Burn limits on Circle's legacy USDC bridge began falling on October 31, and the V1 contracts pause on December 1.

On the same migration page, a block of instructions written for AI coding assistants still says Noble, Sui and Aptos "still require V1." Circle's own release notes say two of those three chains moved to V2 weeks ago.

Circle's legacy cross-chain transfer protocol entered its final month today. From October 31, burn limits on CCTP V1 start falling toward zero, and on December 1 the V1 contracts pause. Any app still using them will stop moving USDC between chains.

Most coverage has focused on those two dates. But the guide developers are told to follow, Circle's V1-to-V2 migration page, contains a mistake in the section written for AI tools.

Embedded in the page is an "Agent Instructions" block, guidance meant for AI coding assistants that read the documentation for developers. It says: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1." For two of those three chains, Circle's other published records say the opposite.

The schedule is fixed. Circle announced in an August 27 blog post that "CCTP V1 (Legacy) deprecation begins October 31, 2026 and completes on December 1, 2026."

From today, V1 burn limits fall, and the migration guide says "message limits will tighten over time until no new burns can be initiated." On December 1 the V1 contracts pause, and any integration still pointing at them can no longer transfer USDC between chains.

Circle has been firm about this. "Migration from CCTP V1 (Legacy) to CCTP V2 is required, not just recommended," the company wrote, adding that V2 "uses separate contracts and APIs and is not backward compatible."

Funds already in transit are protected. The guide says "all pending redemptions will remain available" during the phase-out, and that Circle "will maintain minter allowances greater than the total of pending attestations."

The migration page has two audiences. Human readers see the main guide. AI coding assistants also parse a separate instruction block, which tells them how to answer developer questions.

In that block, the guidance is clear: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1."

The main text above it says something different. According to the human-facing guide, "CCTP V2 contracts are available on all CCTP V1 chains except for Noble and Sui," and "Sui will be supported by V2 before the deprecation begins." Aptos isn't listed as an exception there at all.

So one page gives two different answers about the same chains, and the out-of-date answer is the one written for AI tools.

Circle's 2026 CCTP release notes show how out of date the instruction is:

Circle's supported chains and domains page now lists both Sui and Aptos in its CCTP table, with Standard Transfer support. The page's V1-only section names one chain: Noble.

As of today, Aptos has had V2 for more than two months and Sui for more than three weeks. The instruction telling AI tools that both "still require V1" was overtaken by Circle's own updates before the shutdown began.

Noble is the one chain in that line where the instruction is still accurate, and it is leaving CCTP entirely.

In a September 10 announcement, Circle said "Noble will not receive CCTP V2" and set out its exit:

For Noble, V1 is the only route available, and it is being closed.

A wrong line in documentation would normally be a small issue, but the timing makes this one more serious.

Many developers now ask AI assistants to write or update integration code, and those assistants read documentation like this page. A developer asking how to bridge USDC to Sui or Aptos could be told, based on Circle's own instruction block, to use V1. That is the route whose burn limits started falling today and which pauses in a month.

The fix in the code is not small either. Moving to V2 means:

An integration built on V1 now would have to be rebuilt within weeks.

For teams working with Sui and Aptos, the published records point one way: build on V2, using the contract addresses for domains 8 and 9. Don't follow the V1 guidance from the agent-instruction block.

For Noble, the deadline is January 12, 2027. Before then, integrators need to remove Noble as a CCTP route, and holders need to move or redeem their USDC.

For everyone else, the burn-limit reductions have started. December 1 is the last day V1 integrations work, and any app still on V1 after that will stop moving USDC between chains.

#5294. Binance to Resume XRP, Bitcoin, Ethereum and Other Crypto Withdrawals

Cryptocurrency exchange Binance will allow withdrawals for major cryptocurrencies such as XRP, Bitcoin (BTC), Ethereum (ETH), and Solana (SOL), among others, after suspending withdrawals because of a massive security breach involving $6.3 billion.

Binance announced on Nov. 1 that the exchange would begin resuming withdrawal services between 06:00 and 09:00 UTC.

Binance emphasized that the withdrawal resumption process will be carried out progressively as the exchange conducts security and infrastructure readiness checks.

"We aim to restore withdrawals progressively as we complete security and readiness checks," said Binance.

Binance continued to offer deposit services during the security breach.

The first phase of withdrawal resumption will include a total of 15 blockchain networks.

This list includes popular networks such as Bitcoin, Ethereum, XRP Ledger, BNB Smart Chain, Solana, Tron, and Dogecoin.

Other cryptocurrencies that will be available for withdrawals include Zcash (ZEC), Avalanche (AVAX), Sui (SUI), Polygon (POL) and Arbitrum (ARB).

Withdrawals of major stablecoins such as Tether (USDT) and USD Coin (USDC) will also be enabled on multiple networks.

The exchange noted that it selected the assets based on user withdrawal demand over the past week.

The exchange also warned that not all listed cryptocurrencies and networks may be enabled at the same time.

The withdrawal resumption comes only days after Binance suffered a massive security breach.

The breach led to the theft of around $6.3 billion worth of cryptocurrencies from the exchange's hot wallets.

The exchange temporarily paused withdrawals in order to contain the damage, conduct an investigation into the security breach and avoid additional losses.

Binance has now disclosed that it has recovered around 95% of affected assets.

This is up from 90% when Binance last provided an update on the recovery process.

The exchange said that it has fully backed the balances of cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin, Ethereum, XRP, Solana, BNB, USDT, USDC, Zcash, USD1, and Ripple USD (RLUSD).

The remaining 5% includes cryptocurrencies that are less liquid and harder to buy in large amounts.

Bloomberg Intelligence senior commodity strategist Mike McGlone believes that a critical inflection point for Bitcoin (BTC) versus US Treasury bonds could mean a crash for the broader cryptocurrency market.

In a recent post on X, McGlone cautioned that Bitcoin’s ongoing underperformance against US government bonds may have major implications for other asset classes.

“Bitcoin may be backing down at a key inflection point vs. US Treasury bonds, with broad implications for all assets,” McGlone wrote.

Bitcoin Below $80,000 a Sign of Crypto Breakdown vs. T-Bonds Bitcoin may be backing down from a key inflection point vs. US Treasury bonds, with broad implications for all assets. My graphic highlights the iShares Bitcoin ETF (IBIT) potentially rolling over vs. the iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF (TLT) from a base of 100 at the end of 2024. At 81 on Oct. 30, the IBIT/TLT ratio has been unable to sustain above par since 4Q25 despite IBIT trading at about 4x the volatility of TLT. Bitcoin's dud performance vs. US T-bonds since the end of the milestone year that marked the launch of US ETFs and President Donald Trump's shift to crypto enthusiast from antagonist may signal an end of Bitcoin's glory days. US Treasuries are among the world's most widely leveraged markets, and T-bonds beating Bitcoin for about two years could be a harbinger of what to expect if the crypto stays below $80,000. Full report on the Bloomberg here: https://t.co/OZkRpSxOSs {BI COMD} #Bitcoin #bonds @BBGIntelligence

According to the Bloomberg strategist, $80,000 is a key price level for Bitcoin. He noted that if BTC’s weakness persists below this price, then the cryptocurrency market may face more trouble.

McGlone illustrated his bearish outlook on Bitcoin by comparing BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) with the iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF (TLT).

As of Oct. 30, the IBIT/TLT ratio was at 81, according to McGlone. Here, he set an initial value of 100 at the end of 2024.

This implies that the Bitcoin ETF has underperformed the Treasury bond ETF by roughly 19% on a normalized relative-performance basis during this time.

Furthermore, the IBIT/TLT ratio has struggled to stay above the 100 mark since Q4 of 2025.

Notably, McGlone said that IBIT is about four times as volatile as TLT, so its relative underperformance is alarming.

This is despite Bitcoin's significantly higher volatility. Still, investors holding long-term Treasury bonds have seen better relative performance since the end of 2024.

Meanwhile, Bloomberg’s McGlone also asked if the glory days of Bitcoin could be over.

He mentioned that 2024 was a remarkable year for crypto, with the launch of US spot Bitcoin ETFs and President Donald Trump going from a crypto critic to a vocal supporter.

However, Bitcoin hasn’t outperformed traditional government bonds since then.

Per McGlone, the poor performance of the cryptocurrency may mean its best days are in the past.

#5292. Tron CEO Says Ethereum’s “Fragile Double Top” Prompted Him to Sell 80-90% of ETH Holdings

Sun explained the reason he sold large amounts of his Ether holdings, showcasing his diversification strategy to capitalize on returns in US crypto stocks.

In the Wu Blockchain interview, Justin Sun shared his bold decision to sell 80%-90% of his Ethereum holdings and allocate his portfolio to a selection of US crypto stocks. This comes as the TRON CEO sees massive opportunity in the US market amid what he termed a sluggish performance of Ethereum cryptocurrency.

The founder and CEO of TRON Foundation recently announced that he sold most of his Ethereum holdings. In the recent interview, Justin Sun confirmed that he sold 80%-90% of his personal Ether assets. The interesting event marks his allocation strategy to maximize returns in the US equity market conditions, as he expects US crypto stocks to outperform Ethereum in the near future.

Sun’s decision to withdraw from the market is seen as a personal choice, triggered by what he described as Ethereum’s ‘double top pattern’.  According to the TRON executive, Ether appears to have formed a fragile double top pattern. His clever analysis identified a continuous, bearish pattern that has built a persistent downtrend, which has been hampering profit-making in the ETH market.

The persistence of the ‘fragile double top pattern’ prompted him to cut his Ether positions sharply, while leaving his Bitcoin holdings unchanged, the executive revealed.

Sun’s decision to sell huge chunks of his Ethereum holdings and allocate the funds to US crypto stocks is driven by undervaluation and diversification factors.

He believes that Ethereum is currently non-performing, presenting him with an opportunity to invest the funds in other assets with growth potential. By allocating his Ether funds to US crypto stocks, the renowned investor aims to diversify his portfolio and mitigate risks associated with investing in non-performing assets.

Sun believes that U.S.-listed crypto-related stocks are undervalued, yet have strong market capability. In another Wu Blockchain interview shared earlier today, the TRON CEO revealed his decision to invest in the US-based crypto-related stock, World Liberty Financial (WLFI). In the podcast, he reaffirmed that if given another chance, he would inevitably reinvest in WLFI.

In November 2024, Sun bought $30 million in WLFI tokens, an investment that made him the largest investor in the DeFi platform backed by US President Trump.

Global markets face a packed week of political, economic and corporate events from November 2–6.

U.S. midterm elections could influence future economic policies and cryptocurrency regulations.

Bitcoin has fallen from around $85,000 to $78,299 since the beginning of October, reflecting overall market weakness.

Global markets are heading into a volatile week as investors prepare for the U.S. midterm elections, key economic data, central bank decisions, and earnings from major technology companies.

The events come as a tech-led sell-off has wiped out roughly $5 trillion in market value across major technology and semiconductor stocks since early October, making this week’s events crucial to watch.

The week begins with the U.S. ISM Manufacturing PMI for October, expected to rise to 54.8 from 54.5 in September. A reading above 50 signals growth in the manufacturing sector, while a weaker result could put pressure on the U.S. dollar.

Apple and Palantir Technologies will also report earnings after the U.S. market closes. Apple is expected to post around $113.4 billion in fiscal Q4 2026 revenue, compared with $109.42 billion in the previous quarter.

Palantir is expected to report about $2.18 billion in Q3 2026 revenue, up from $1.94 billion in the previous quarter.

Tuesday brings one of the week’s biggest political events as the U.S. midterm elections are scheduled to be held. All 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats are up for election.

The result could influence President Donald Trump’s economic agenda, government spending, and future financial regulation.

For the crypto industry, the result matters because Congress will decide the direction of future digital asset laws and oversee regulators such as the SEC and CFTC.

On the same day, the September JOLTS report is expected to be released, which is expected to show around 7.11 million job openings, compared with 7.079 million in the previous report. A higher figure could point to strong labor demand and add to concerns about wage growth and inflation.

Meanwhile, AMD, Arista Networks, Astera Labs, Shopify and Eaton are scheduled to report earnings.

Wednesday brings two major economic reports. The ADP National Employment Report is expected to show 65,000 new private-sector jobs. A lower figure could point to slower hiring.

Alongside this job data, eurozone inflation is expected to increase to 3.9% in October from 3.8% in September. The previous increase was already significant, with inflation rising from 3.2% in August. Another increase could add pressure on the European Central Bank to keep interest rates high.

Earnings reports from Qualcomm, Arm, AppLovin, Coherent, Uber and Datadog are also scheduled for the days.

The Bank of England’s interest-rate decision will be Thursday’s main event. In September, the central bank held its Bank Rate at 3.75%, although three of its nine policymakers voted for a 0.25-percentage-point increase to 4%.

Markets are now expecting a possible rate hike to 4%, which would signal continued concern about inflation despite pressure on economic growth.

On the same day, the U.S. will also release its weekly jobless claims data. Initial claims are expected to remain near multi-decade lows, following a drop to 194,000 in the previous week.

Microchip Technology, Lumentum, Cloudflare and Airbnb are also scheduled to report earnings.

Friday’s October employment report could be the week’s most important economic release.

U.S. employers are expected to have added around 60,000 jobs in October, up from 29,000 in September. The unemployment rate is forecast to remain unchanged at 4.2%.

The report will show whether the U.S. labour market is stabilising or continuing to weaken.

Global markets entered November under pressure from concerns over tech-stock valuations, AI spending and interest rates. Hedge fund selling added to the pressure, putting this week’s earnings in focus.

Last week, the S&P 500 fell 0.6% to 7,580.07, while the Nasdaq dropped 2% to 25,437. China’s Shanghai Composite fell 1.61% to 3,599, while the CSI 300 recorded an 8.5% loss in October.

Meanwhile, Japan’s Nikkei 225 gained around 0.95% for the week to trade near 63,081.

Crypto markets have also come under pressure. Bitcoin has fallen from around $85,000 at the start of October to $78,299.35, although it is slightly higher today.

Fed meeting today: markets give a hold 95% odds and a December hike 79%. What traders expect from Warsh and what it means for Bitcoin.

The Federal Reserve is expected to keep its policy rate at 3.75% to 4.00% when its two-day Fed meeting ends on Wednesday, October 28, as officials weigh 3.7% inflation against a weakening job market six days before the U.S. midterms. Polymarket traders give a hold 94.9% odds ahead of the 2 p.m. ET statement. The decision itself is mostly priced in. December isn’t: the same markets see a 79% chance of another hike then, so crypto traders will be watching Chair Kevin Warsh’s press conference at 2:30 p.m. more than the statement.

Bitcoin trades at $81,430, up 1.9% in 24 hours.

A hold is close to certain, and the betting is now on December. Prediction markets, futures and economists line up:

Polymarket’s October market alone has drawn $86 million in bets. Its most likely three-meeting path, at 59%, is a hold today, a hike in December and a hold in January. The December figures add the 25 and 50 basis-point hike markets on each platform.

The bond market agrees. The two-year Treasury yield stood at 4.68% on Monday, 68 basis points above the top of the Fed’s range and up from 4.17% in late August. Traders don’t demand that much more than the Fed pays unless they expect it to keep raising rates.

A hawkish hold: no move today, but no promise of a pause either. The case for waiting is that the data are pulling in two directions. September’s consumer prices rose 3.7% from a year earlier, up from 3.4% in August, with Brent crude still near $111 a barrel. At the same time, employers added just 29,000 jobs in September and unemployment rose to 4.2%.

The Fed raised rates by a quarter point on September 16, by a 12–0 vote. Its statement said inflation was still too high and that “the Committee will deliver price stability.” Warsh has largely avoided forward guidance as chair and has said he doesn’t “prejudge meetings.”

The number to watch is the dissents. Cleveland’s Beth Hammack, Dallas’s Lorie Logan and Minneapolis’s Neel Kashkari voted for a hike in July, when the rest of the committee held. On Polymarket, two dissents are the most likely outcome at 33.5%, ahead of three (28%) and none (23%). Matt Weller of FOREX.com calls two or more dissents a “true hawkish hold,” while zero would cast doubt on December.

Timing adds a political layer. “The Fed doesn’t want to poke the White House in the eye six days before an election,” SMBC chief economist Joseph LaVorgna said ahead of the meeting.

The most plausible outcome is a hold with two hawkish dissents, a statement that again calls inflation too high, and a press conference in which Warsh keeps December open without committing to it. That would leave the December odds roughly where they are, between 73% and 79%. The bigger surprise risk is on the dovish side: no dissents, or Warsh arguing that 5% ten-year yields are already doing the Fed’s work.

History this year says the reaction matters more than the decision. Bitcoin fell in the 24 hours after three of the five holds in 2026, by an average of 2.6% across all five, with the biggest drops after January (−6.2%) and June (−5.1%). The one hike, on September 16, was followed by a 1.1% gain in a day and 11.3% in a week, as the uncertainty that had built up before it cleared.

Bitcoin after each 2026 Fed decision. Source: Binance

Options traders aren’t expecting much this time. Deribit’s DVOL index, which tracks the 30-day volatility implied by Bitcoin options, stood at 37.3 on Wednesday and has stayed between about 37 and 39 for the past two weeks. That leaves room for a surprise in either direction. A firm signal for December would lift yields and the dollar, which has tended to weigh on Bitcoin. A softer Warsh would do the opposite.

The calendar doesn’t end tonight. September’s PCE inflation and third-quarter GDP arrive on Thursday, Deribit’s monthly options expire on Friday, and the midterms follow on November 3.

Bitcoin has some room above its moving averages but hasn’t retaken October’s open. It trades at $81,430 on Binance, above its 50-day exponential moving average (EMA) at $80,829 and the 200-day EMA at $76,442.

Today’s Fed meeting is expected to end in a hold. What moves markets will be the dissents and Warsh’s answers about December, and Thursday’s PCE report will show whether the inflation case for a hike is getting stronger.

#5289. Do Not Use Your iPhone as Hardware Wallet, OneKey Founder

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

Using an old iPhone as a crypto cold wallet may be less safe than it looks, OneKey founder Yishi Wang has warned. The practice is popular with self-custody fans: wipe a spare phone, take it offline, and keep your wallet recovery information on it.

Wang's worry is that an offline phone can still be attacked by someone who has it in their hands. He has pointed to flaws in several generations of iPhone. These include the publicly documented checkm8 issue on older models and, more recently reported, low-level weaknesses in certain later devices. They sit in the early stages of the boot process. A malicious app isn't involved.

An iOS update may not fix a weakness built into immutable boot code. Switching off Wi-Fi and cellular does nothing about someone who gets physical access to the phone. A vulnerability still doesn't automatically mean an attacker can recover a seed phrase, though. Device encryption, passcode strength and secure key handling remain real barriers.

Wang advises against trusting iPhone 11-generation and older devices with recovery phrases. If you think a phrase may have been exposed, create a completely new one using a trusted setup and move your funds to that wallet. Generating another address from the same seed won't help, because the underlying exposure stays.

He also stresses updated operating systems, long alphanumeric passcodes and careful control of USB connections. Earlier, he suggested that even newer iPhones shouldn't be treated as equivalent to purpose-built signing devices when the holdings are substantial and long-term.

Dedicated hardware wallets are built to isolate signing keys and let you check transaction details on the device itself. They carry risk too. Counterfeit hardware, compromised distribution channels and sloppy recovery-phrase handling can all undermine their security.

The argument is about threat models, not brand loyalty. An offline phone cuts remote exposure, but that doesn't turn it into a secure hardware wallet.

#5287. Akash’s Solana Migration Clears November 2 Vote at 97%, With Four More On-Chain Decisions Ahead

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

AKT stakers are close to approving Akash's move from Cosmos to Solana, with Mintscan projecting a pass at 97.2% yes as voting enters its final hours.

But a yes on Proposal 346 opens a door rather than completing a move. Before a single AKT reaches Solana, two independent audits and at least two more on-chain votes still have to happen.

The summary going around is simple: Akash is leaving Cosmos for Solana. The proposal itself is narrower than that, and the details matter for anyone holding AKT.

Proposal 346 on akashnet-2, titled "Migrate the Akash Protocol to Solana," closes at 15:02 UTC on November 2. A yes vote approves the migration plan and authorises AKT to launch as an SPL token through a one-way portal that stays open for two years. It does not set a cutover date, it does not move a single lease, and on its own it does not open the portal.

The technical spec for that portal was published the day after voting opened. It shows how many further steps lie between this vote and a working SPL AKT.

The proposal text in Akash's AEP repository says a yes vote does two things:

It also says plainly what it doesn't do: "it does not set a cutover date and does not move the marketplace." Live leases, staking and governance on akashnet-2 continue as normal. The marketplace moves only after audits and rehearsals pass and "a separate cutover proposal passes on this chain."

A no vote would stop the whole plan. In the proposal's words: "Nothing moves; the token does not launch and the program returns to option analysis."

At 08:43 UTC on November 2, about six hours before voting closed, Mintscan's page for Proposal 346 showed an expected result of "Will PASS":

Turnout stood at 68.80% of bonded stake, against a quorum of 33.40%. The same figures can be read from Akash's own chain API, through the proposal object and its tally endpoint.

Mintscan's 97.2% is yes as a share of all votes cast. Akash's pass threshold leaves abstentions out, and on that basis yes stands at about 98.7%, far above the 50% needed. The veto share is negligible.

The tally has barely changed since early morning. A read of the chain at 07:29 UTC showed almost exactly the same totals, with only a handful of AKT added to the yes side. With turnout and margin that large, the outcome is not in doubt. The more useful question is what happens after it passes.

The portal's design is in AEP-95, "One-Way AKT Sink to Solana,", a draft published on October 27 by core developers Artur Troian and Joseph Chalabi. It describes a "deliberately one-way" bridge with no return path. The authors say this removes "the largest class of bridge attacks."

Why supply doesn't change: every SPL AKT is backed by AKT locked on Akash, and nothing is minted independently on Solana. The token is a legacy SPL mint with six decimals and no freeze authority.

The spec's own risk table names the biggest trust point. The upgrade authority over the Solana programs could "mint without limit." That power is meant to sit with a time-locked multisig appointed by Akash governance, with monitors set to alert on every admin action.

At launch, SPL AKT has no protocol role. It will support "transfers and DEX liquidity only, with no staking or governance rights." Inflation stays on Akash. To seed trading, Overclock Labs, Akash's core developer, will send 1 million AKT through the bridge to a Solana treasury vault. That deposit follows the same rules as everyone else's.

Proposal 346 requires "two independent audits of the token and portal code before launch," with reports published within 30 days. AEP-95's launch sequence shows what that requirement means on-chain.

So Proposal 346 is the first of at least five on-chain decisions. The "2 to 3 weeks" launch estimate depends on the audits finishing and the upgrade and parameter votes passing on schedule.

For now, nothing. The proposal's disclosures set out what changes later:

Discussion of the proposal continues in GitHub Discussion #1123.

The proposal lists four items as "still open, to be settled and published before the cutover proposal":

The second item matters most to holders. The portal closes two years after launch, and the proposal doesn't yet say what happens to AKT that hasn't crossed by then. The final tally will confirm whether the plan goes ahead, but that answer, and the decisions in the votes that follow, will matter more to most holders than today's margin.

Ripple's scheduled November escrow unlock has put 1 billion XRP into circulation, with blockchain data tracker Whale Alert reporting two transactions in this regard.

According to Whale Alert, 500,000,000 XRP (626,430,089 USD) was unlocked at Ripple in the early hours of November 1; another 500,000,000 XRP (626,430,089 USD) was unlocked, bringing the total unlock to 1 billion XRP tokens.

🔓 🔓 🔓 🔓 🔓 🔓 🔓 🔓 🔓 🔓 500,000,000 $XRP (626,430,089 USD) unlocked at #Ripple https://t.co/ejC9qFmsjb

Ripple's monthly unlocks are part of the firm's ongoing process to increase transparency and predictability around XRP distribution. The company initially put 55 billion XRP in escrow and released it in an organized fashion over time to manage the supply of XRP entering circulation.

But not all of the 1 billion XRP that was released stays on the market. In the past, Ripple has returned a large portion of the unlocked XRP (about 700 million XRP) to escrow while keeping some of it to facilitate operational needs, liquidity, and ecosystem-related activities.

October was a big month for Ripple and the XRP ecosystem, as it saw a slew of announcements and updates for the XRP Ledger. It also hosted two of the largest events for XRP and Ripple: Swell and the XRP Seoul events.

RLUSD was listed on Coinbase in October, allowing retail and institutional clients to trade and manage RLUSD through Coinbase Prime, Coinbase Exchange, and the Coinbase Retail app, with 1:1 conversion from U.S. dollars and other supported USD-denominated stablecoins into RLUSD.

The XRP Ledger is set for crucial fixes and improvements over the next few days. According to XRPScan data, fixCleanup3_4_0, which began its two-week activation window on Oct 21, 2026, after a reset in voting, now eyes the earliest activation date being 2:46 PM UTC on Nov 4, 2026.

Validator support for the fixCleanup3_4_0 amendment must stay above 80% for it to activate. If it slips to 80% or lower even once, the amendment is rejected and the 14-day timer starts over.

This fixCleanup3_4_0 amendment is a collection of fixes for Single Asset Vaults, the Lending Protocol, Automated Market Makers, the permissioned DEX, trust lines, NFTs, MPTs, Escrow, Sponsorship, transaction signing, and permission delegation.

The fixCleanup3_4_0 amendment is essential for Permission Delegation, which went live in October, as until it is enabled, users would not be able to delegate the PaymentBurn granular permission.

#5285. Bitcoin ETFs Take In $424 Million, but BTC Slips Below $80,000: What Bitcoin News Could November Bring?

Bitcoin news: ETFs took in $424M in three days, yet BTC fell under $80,000 after a split Fed hold. Bitcoin rose in only 3 of 8 Novembers.

U.S. spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds took in $137.3 million on Wednesday, October 28, their third straight day of inflows, while the Federal Reserve held interest rates at 3.75% to 4% and two of its officials voted for a hike. The buying didn’t hold the price for long. Bitcoin rose to $81,788 after the decision, then fell to $79,710 overnight as a selloff in chip stocks spread to crypto.

BTC trades at $79,899, down 1.2% in 24 hours and 4.4% for October, which is on track to be its second losing October in a row. For traders following Bitcoin news into November, the calendar is crowded: the midterm elections, fresh jobs and inflation data, and a December rate hike that prediction markets now price at 79%.

So what do the ETF flows, the Fed and November’s record say?

Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack voted for an increase. pic.twitter.com/nUKDM6n8Zp

— Nick Timiraos (@NickTimiraos) October 28, 2026

DISCOVER: Meme coin supercycle: Top performers this week

About $424 million in three sessions. SoSoValue’s daily figures show almost all of it went through BlackRock:

The run follows a rough patch. On October 22 the funds lost $635.6 million in a day, their biggest outflow since June, with IBIT and Fidelity’s FBTC each shedding more than $200 million. Through Monday, October was still about $202 million in the red. The two days since have tipped it slightly positive, by roughly $110 million.

The 12 funds now hold $104.9 billion, about 6.4% of all Bitcoin by value, and have taken in $57.6 billion net since they launched in January 2024. IBIT alone holds $66.1 billion.

A hold, but not a quiet one. The Fed’s statement passed 10–2, with Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack voting for a quarter-point hike. It said the economy is “expanding at a strong pace” and inflation is still too high, and it left the next step to “the accumulation of more information.”

Chair Kevin Warsh gave no hint about December. “I don’t believe in forward guidance, absent exigent circumstances, absent a crisis,” he told reporters, adding that politics “played no role” six days before the midterms. Traders read the dissents as a lean toward tightening. Polymarket’s December market prices a quarter-point hike at 77%, about where it stood before the meeting.

Bitcoin took the decision calmly at first. It traded at $80,860 at 2 p.m. ET and rose 1.1% to $81,788 over the next two hours. The drop came later, during Asian trading, after Samsung’s chip unit missed analysts’ estimates and its shares fell more than 5%, pulling tech stocks lower.

BTC fell to $79,710 by 02:00 UTC, and more than $350 million in leveraged crypto bets were liquidated over 24 hours.

A month of data that will decide whether December’s hike happens. The dates to watch:

November’s reputation as a strong month for Bitcoin rests mostly on two years. On Binance, BTC rose in only three of the last eight Novembers. The big gains, 42.8% in 2020 and 37.2% in 2024, both came right after presidential elections. The two midterm years, 2018 and 2022, ended November down 36.6% and 16.2%.

Bitcoin’s November returns since 2018. Source: Binance

Eight years is a small sample, and both midterm Novembers fell in the middle of bear markets. Options traders aren’t betting on a big move either way. Deribit’s DVOL index, which tracks the 30-day volatility implied by Bitcoin options, stood at 36.5 on Wednesday, just under the 37 to 39 range it held for the previous two weeks.

It is testing the area now. BTC trades at $79,899 on Binance, back under its 50-day exponential moving average (EMA) at $80,789, a line it has crossed three times in the past week. The October 24 low of $79,221 is the floor that has held so far.

The one-year view is steadier than the week. The 200-day EMA has climbed from about $72,300 in late August to $76,476, and the 50-day crossed above it on September 12, the first such cross since it fell below in November 2025.

The ETF buyers came back this week, but the Fed left December open and the price is still hostage to tech stocks. For Bitcoin news in the days ahead, the first test is today’s PCE report, and the next is the November 6 jobs data.

#5284. Near Protocol (NEAR) Hits $1.1 Billion in Open Interest, Breaks Threshold For First Time Since September

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

A reported $1.1 billion in NEAR Protocol derivatives open interest has put the spotlight on speculative positioning in the token. The exact figure and its timing need confirmation at the exchange level. The general point holds either way: leveraged trading magnifies both optimism and downside when interest in an asset picks up.

Open interest is the notional value of futures and perpetual futures contracts that are still open. Daily trading volume is something else, a count of transactions over a period. Rising open interest means more positions are staying active. It doesn't say whether traders as a group expect prices to rise or fall, since every contract has exposure on both sides.

NEAR's derivatives participation has been swining before. In October open interest climbed above $1 billion and approached $1.9 billion during a strong price rally, then a pullback.

To read a fresh increase, analysts usually compare open interest with spot price, funding rates, trading volume and liquidation data. When price and open interest rise together, the market often reads that as growing risk appetite. If prices fall while open interest stays high, crowded leveraged positions become vulnerable to forced exits.

Funding rates are just another source of data. Sustained positive funding can suggest stronger demand for leveraged longs, and negative funding a preference for shorts. Neither is conclusive alone, and differences between exchanges can muddy comparisons.

NEAR's longer-term prospects depend on more than derivatives. Transaction costs, ecosystem integrations and adoption of cross-chain infrastructure such as NEAR Intents are more longer-term drivers. Speculative positioning can move the price fast, but it is no substitute for durable demand for blockchain services.

New leveraged positions must be backed by spot-market buying and healthy liquidity in order to have relevance. A large open-interest figure shows attention, nothing more. It isn't a forecast. Check it across data providers and manage risk carefully.

#5282. Chainlink Goes Live on Stellar, Unlocking DeFi Applications Across the $4B RWA Ecosystem

By accessing highly reliable and accurate market data through the Chainlink oracle, Stellar unlocks greater DeFi applications to meet its RWA utilities.

In a groundbreaking move to accelerate the transition to the on-chain financial ecosystem, Stellar Network today announced the integration of Chainlink into its protocol. In a blog post published today, Stellar revealed that it has adopted Chainlink’s data feeds as its official oracle solution.

Stellar Network is a decentralized blockchain network recognized for facilitating rapid, cheap, and secure cross-border payments and fund transfer applications for institutions and individuals. However, one shortcoming of traditional blockchains, like Stellar Network and several others, is their inability to access real-world data directly. Stellar aims to address this by adopting Chainlink oracles.

Chainlink oracles are specialized smart contracts that bridge blockchain networks and external data sources. They enable reliable and secure exchange of real-world data (like asset prices) to and from blockchain smart contracts. By adopting Chainlink oracles, Stellar expands the capabilities of its blockchain infrastructure, allowing it to interact with off-chain data in a trustless, decentralized manner.

Chainlink’s price feed is a crucial blockchain instrument that connects smart contracts and real-world data. Many DeFi applications across chains rely on these price feeds to keep their services running smoothly.

As a result, by adopting Chainlink’s oracle, Stellar aims to expand its protocol’s capabilities. This means that Stellar’s DeFi ecosystem now has access to reliable pricing data through Chainlink’s scale program.

The oracle integration is set to unlock a new level of DeFi adoption on Stellar. With Chainlink’s data streams and data feeds now available on Stellar, developers have access to the market data needed to build on-chain applications that connect Stellar’s advancing RWA ecosystem with DeFi.

Stellar’s blockchain already supports $4+ billion in RWAs, with assets moving on-chain. The incorporation of a Chainlink oracle ensures assets are priced, traded, used as collateral, and borrowed against reliably. With the integration, liquidity and assets on Stellar become part of a productive DeFi ecosystem where customers put their capital (e.g., tokenized stocks, stablecoins, and various assets) to work.

#5281. MIKA Crypto Crashes 99% After Influencer Posts Her Dev Wallet’s Private Key: Are Celebrity Tokens Back, and Does Anyone Need Them?

An influencer posted her dev wallet key, not the token address, and MIKA crypto crashed in minutes. After LAPTOP, are celebrity tokens back?

Crypto influencer Mika (@mikadontlouz) posted what traders say was her token’s developer wallet private key instead of its contract address. The MIKA crypto token she had just launched crashed about 99% in a single sale minutes later.

For an account with 126,000 followers, that is the equivalent of tweeting your bank PIN with the caption “free yourselves.” Which, as it happens, is roughly what the post said.

Half an hour later she launched again, this time with one wallet holding half the supply. That one is down about 84% from its peak. Bad luck, a botched launch or a tidy exit with a ready-made excuse?

And while we’re asking: after Hunter Biden’s LAPTOP token went the same way in September, are celebrity tokens back, and does anyone actually need them?

Mika just tried to launch a pump coin and instead of tweeting the CA she tweeted the devs wallet private key instead…😭 pic.twitter.com/pjsA0vY7bl

Two launches, two crashes, one afternoon. More or less this is the timeline:

The relaunch now sits at a market cap of about $240,000, with $41,700 of liquidity and $1.65 million traded in 24 hours. The internet, meanwhile, did what it does: DexScreener lists more than a dozen copycats with names like Free Mika King, Jail Mika and Mute Mika.

Maybe. But it was a very specific kind of mistake. Copying a private key instead of a contract address means opening the wallet’s export screen, revealing a string twice as long as the one you meant to share, and pasting it under a caption that starts with “free yourselves.” Plenty of people in crypto have done dumber things. Few have done them with such good copywriting.

Ouhhhh man I'm tired@mikadontlouz "accidentally" posted her private key and "lost $40K"

(was fake.. she put a nonce on the wallet before posting it)

– 400k spawner– dev holds 50%– awful bubblemaps pic.twitter.com/TSsTj8LdFC

— fabiano.sol (@FabianoSolana) October 28, 2026

Whether it was an outsider who copied the key or an existing owner is still unknown, and from the transaction alone the two are hard to tell apart.

To be fair to Mika, none of this proves she meant it. A rushed launch, a clipboard mix-up and a panicked relaunch would leave a similar trail. But a leak that hands the blame for the dump to “whoever copied the key,” a claimed $40,000 loss that may not have happened, and a relaunch where one wallet held half the tokens add up to a lot of coincidences for one afternoon.

DISCOVER: PUMP vs FOMO: Can Signing $40M TRUMP Trader Kimchi Help Pump.fun Win the Launchpad War?

They never really left, they just keep ending the same way. The latest big one came seven weeks ago. Hunter Biden’s LAPTOP token launched on Base on September 9 and jumped to $190.81 two minutes in, on a pool holding about $48,000 of liquidity, then fell to $3.70 within the hour. Biden blamed a market maker and denied his team sold. Bubblemaps found about 80% of LAPTOP traders ended up underwater.

But that is just one in a long list of failed launches by these “celebrities”:

Celebrity tokens, drop from all-time high. Source: CoinGecko

The pattern barely changes. A famous name brings the buyers, insiders or snipers own a large share of the supply, liquidity is thin, and the chart looks like a ski jump. The famous name moves on to the next interview. The people who bought the third green candle don’t.

Short answer: the buyers apparently think so, the charts disagree. A celebrity token has no product, no cash flow and, in most cases, no plan beyond launch day. What it sells is access to a name, and that lasts about as long as the first big holder’s patience.

The tools for spotting trouble keep getting better, too. A Bubblemaps holder map showed the relaunch’s 50% wallet within the hour, and on-chain sleuths had the nonce account screenshotted before the Spaces ended. The second token still traded $1.65 million in 24 hours.

MIKA crypto will probably be forgotten by next week, replaced by the next name with a ticker. If there is a lesson, it’s the oldest one in memecoins: when someone posts “its time to eat,” check who is setting the table.

The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. The cryptocurrency market is breaking the classical rules of financial economics. The industry has faced the biggest challenge in its history: the FBI confirmed that North Korean hackers attacked Binance's infrastructure and withdrew $6.3 billion.

However, instead of a protracted capitulation, this news triggered a paradoxical reaction: prices held, creating a strong bullish precedent.

Against this backdrop, well-known crypto analyst DonAlt, who accurately predicted the historic 700% XRP rally back in 2024, directly cites the Binance hack as the reason for his ultra-bullish sentiment. In his opinion, in the current situation it is "hard to be a bear" precisely because of how the market reacted to the catastrophe.

The situation was promptly stabilized by the actions of the platform itself, which acted proactively and covered 90% of users' lost funds from its own reserves, and by the Treasury Department. As a result, Bitcoin ignored attempts at mass sell-offs and held around $77,935, while XRP settled at $1.2498.

The main indicator for the analyst was the complete absence of panic follow-through selling after the shocking news. DonAlt draws a direct analogy with the events of November 2022, when the industry was going through the collapse of the FTX exchange:

"Last time the market didn't properly sell off after a huge event like this was the FTX collapse. When I saw the lack of follow through then I got giga bullish. And we subsequently went from 16k to 100k. Hard to be bearish here after having been given the same setup yet again"

The expert emphasizes that there are no 100% guarantees in financial markets and classifies the current situation as a game of mathematical probabilities. According to him, when the market prices in colossal negativity but refuses to go down, the odds in the long run are always on the side of buyers.

Still, DonAlt’s argument rests on a single precedent. The FTX analogy worked once, but one case is not a pattern, and the two events differ in important ways. FTX wiped out customer funds for good, while in the Binance case most losses were covered within days.

A market that does not fall on a compensated hack is responding rationally, not necessarily showing hidden strength.

The real test will come in the next few weeks: if prices hold once the news is fully priced in and attention shifts to the stolen funds moving through mixers, the bullish case gets much stronger. If they don’t, the lack of follow-through may turn out to have been only a delay.

#5279. Why Didn't Bitcoin Drop More? Binance's CZ Credits FBI

Binance founder Changpeng Zhao (CZ) credited the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and other US law enforcement agencies with helping prevent a larger drop in the Bitcoin (BTC) price after the massive $6.3 billion security breach at the Binance cryptocurrency exchange.

Binance founder CZ commended the timely actions of the FBI, US Secret Service (USSS), and Internal Revenue Service (IRS) amid the massive security breach.

According to CZ's Nov. 1 post on X, US law enforcement agencies (FBI, USSS, IRS and more) helped "a lot" during the incident.

For instance, they helped with tracking and freezing funds.

According to the Binance co-founder, they were able to prevent an even sharper fall in the Bitcoin price.

"Not enough to express our appreciation in a tweet. There are probably a lot of crypto bros not realizing that a lot of 'why bitcoin didn't drop even more?' credits go to them," CZ stated.

This comes after the FBI officially identified North Korean hackers as being behind the record-breaking Binance hack.

According to the FBI's Oct. 31 announcement, North Korea stole more than $6 billion worth of cryptocurrencies from the Binance crypto exchange on or about Oct. 29.

More specifically, the FBI identified the North Korean cybercrime group TraderTraitor as being behind the massive cryptocurrency theft.

It's a known North Korean hacker group that has stolen large amounts of cryptocurrencies before.

The FBI noted that investigators, together with the Secret Service and IRS Criminal Investigation, have tracked how the hackers were exchanging stolen cryptocurrencies mainly for Ethereum (ETH).

The FBI warned that these assets could be further laundered using decentralized finance (DeFi) protocols and instant cryptocurrency swap services.

The US authorities have called on cryptocurrency businesses and infrastructure providers to block transactions related to the cryptocurrency addresses used by the hackers to stop them from laundering these assets.

Specifically, the US authorities urged THORNode operators, remote procedure call (RPC) node operators, instant exchanges, blockchain analytics companies, DeFi platforms, etc., to block such transactions.

Apart from that, the FBI provided a list of the cryptocurrency addresses used by the hackers to allow other members of the cryptocurrency industry to detect and block suspicious transactions.

The Binance security breach sent shock waves throughout the cryptocurrency market.

Bitcoin tumbled below $77,000 after the market reacted to the unprecedented crypto theft.

BTC dropped to around $76,000 at one point, registering its lowest price in several weeks.

Meanwhile, other major cryptocurrencies like Ethereum, XRP, Solana (SOL), and BNB nosedived as the market reacted to the breach.

Fortunately, Bitcoin eventually found stability and was trading around $78,000 during the early Nov. 1 trading session.

Prediction markets give Democrats roughly a 70% chance of taking control of both chambers of Congress.

A potential Democratic majority could complicate negotiations over the CLARITY Act and reshape the regulatory outlook for crypto.

AI bailout proposals and the risk of renewed US-Iran strikes add further uncertainty for stocks, oil and global markets.

The US midterm elections on November 3 could become a major market catalyst, with investors watching beyond the battle for control of Congress. Prediction markets currently give Democrats around a 70% chance of winning both the House and Senate. The outcome could influence the direction of AI regulation, the future of crypto legislation and US foreign policy toward Iran.

For financial markets, the election carries implications across technology stocks, digital assets, energy prices and inflation. Here are three developments investors should watch as voters head to the polls.

Artificial intelligence has become one of the biggest investment themes on Wall Street, but concerns over elevated valuations, rising infrastructure costs and debt-funded expansion are putting the sector under scrutiny.

On October 29, Democratic lawmakers Maxine Waters and Greg Casar introduced a resolution opposing federal bailouts for AI companies if an AI-related market bubble collapses. The proposal argues that taxpayers should not be required to rescue companies or executives responsible for excessive risk-taking. It also calls for stronger protections for workers, retirees and households exposed to a potential downturn.

A stronger Democratic presence in Congress could increase pressure for greater oversight of AI companies and their financing arrangements. That could add another regulatory consideration for major technology firms investing billions of dollars in data centers, chips and AI infrastructure.

The election could also determine how quickly the US advances comprehensive cryptocurrency regulation. The CLARITY Act, designed to establish a clearer regulatory framework for digital assets, failed to advance in the Senate on September 15. The measure received 49 votes in favor and 50 against, falling short of the 60 votes required. All Democrats and four Republicans opposed advancing the legislation.

A change in congressional control could make negotiations more complicated, particularly if lawmakers disagree over the regulatory responsibilities of the SEC and CFTC, oversight of crypto markets and the treatment of digital asset businesses.

For the crypto industry, regulatory clarity remains an important factor in attracting institutional participation and encouraging US-based companies to expand. A prolonged legislative delay could keep uncertainty elevated for exchanges, token issuers and other digital asset businesses.

Bitcoin and major altcoins may therefore remain sensitive to signals about the next stage of US crypto policy. However, the election outcome alone will not determine the bill’s future; bipartisan support will still be necessary for major legislation to advance.

The geopolitical risk surrounding the election could have an immediate impact on energy markets. US officials have reportedly warned several Middle Eastern allies to prepare for possible renewed military strikes against Iran after November 3. The warnings also include concerns about potential Iranian retaliation against energy facilities and other critical infrastructure. President Donald Trump has not made a final decision on further military action, while diplomatic efforts remain possible.

Any renewed escalation could threaten regional energy infrastructure and disrupt oil supply routes. The Strait of Hormuz remains particularly important because of its role in global energy shipments. Oil markets are already facing considerable supply uncertainty. Brent crude recently settled above $113 per barrel, while US crude traded near $104, with geopolitical tensions and shipping risks adding to market pressure.

A fresh conflict could push oil prices higher, increasing transportation and production costs and adding pressure to global inflation. That could complicate the Federal Reserve’s policy decisions and weigh on risk-sensitive assets, including equities and cryptocurrencies.

The November 3 election will provide the first indication of how political control in Washington could change, but its market implications will extend beyond the initial results.

A Democratic victory in both chambers could bring tougher scrutiny of AI financing and complicate negotiations over crypto legislation. Meanwhile, the possibility of renewed military action against Iran creates a separate risk for oil supplies, inflation and global market sentiment.

For investors, the key will be how quickly these political developments translate into policy decisions. Technology stocks, crypto assets and energy markets could each respond differently, making the election an important event for financial markets heading into the final months of 2026 and beyond.
